news.title: Scott Colom Wins Mississippi, Becomes State's 1st Black Senator Since 1874
news.text: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any US state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi."While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," Hyde-Smith, 67, said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."A spokesman for the senator said she called Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.READ | Saba Haider Credits Ghaziabad Upbringing For Her Public Life, US WinColom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson.The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term."They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society."It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America - a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.Party leaders hailed the senator-elect's triumph, with nods to the South's emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas."Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done," Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. "Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what's possible for Democrats in the South."Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won "because you believe in the promise of your state's people. And they believed in you right back."Vera Finley was among those supporters, and she arrived early Wednesday to Colom's victory party."I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields," Finley said. "Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history."Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state's voters "made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out.""In a state that has witnessed some of the nation's most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy," Johnson said.Despite Schumer's support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see Mississippi as winnable.The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.He produced of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead."When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?"Then she stepped away.Colom's appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump's policies - especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers - without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington - a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.There is some irony to Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a US District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Governor Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family."In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction."He was killed for helping Mississippians vote," Colom said. "On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right."Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Governor Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.Then-Governor Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former US agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story."My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values," he said, "and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I've done that they shouldn't get a chance."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Trump's Veterans Day Message Compared to Those of Potential 2028 Contenders
news.text: President Donald Trump used his Veterans Day address at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday to honor U.S. service members while highlighting his administration's military record, veterans policies and foreign policy priorities. Trump praised the sacrifices of those who served in uniform and said Americans owed an enduring debt to veterans. "On Veterans Day, we honor those who have worn the uniform, who have worn the battle, who have stood to watch, whose ranks have formed the mighty wall of flesh and blood, of bravery and devotion that has defended our freedom for 250 years," Trump said. He pointed to record military recruiting numbers, improvements in veterans' care and America's renewed strength on the world stage as accomplishments of his administration. "Our republic has triumphed, and today our country is stronger than it has ever been before," Trump said. The president referenced U.S. operations involving Iran and Venezuela, argued that American military power had been restored under his leadership and contrasted his administration's handling of veterans' issues with that of previous administrations. He also touted his most recent construction project. “Soon, we’re going to dedicate a magnificent triumphal arch to our veterans,” Trump told the crowd at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia. “And that’s in honor of our great veterans and our great military. They’ve been waiting for it for 200 years." Potential 2028 Republican Contenders Although the 2028 Republican presidential race has yet to take shape, Vice President JD Vance has consistently been viewed as an early front-runner in polling and prediction markets. Other Republicans frequently mentioned as potential contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis. This is not a comprehensive list. JD Vance Vance, who served in the U.S. Marine Corps from 2003 to 2007, recognized three World War II veterans alongside Trump at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday. “One of the most important things our veterans do is not just fight for their country; they fight for their fellow veterans," Vance told the crowd. "And let me say, as one veteran to the next, we are picking up that torch every single day. We will never leave our veterans behind.” Marco Rubio Rubio, who is in Paris for the G7 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, released a video message on One America News Network, urging Americans to care for military members and their families. "There is no higher calling for a citizen than defense of country, but in America today, it is a duty shouldered by less than 1 percent of our total population," he said in part. Ron DeSantis The term-limited governor of Florida is reportedly setting up a conservative think tank and considering whether to make a 2028 bid, after suspending his 2024 presidential run. He said service members should be honored for being willing to make the ultimate sacrifice for their country. "Anyone who puts on the cloth of our country is sacrificing for something bigger than any individual," the governor posted to X in part. Glenn Youngkin Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin, who has success in a state that has trended Democratic, is frequently mentioned as a potential Republican contender in early 2028 discussions. He marked Veterans Day by honoring the service and sacrifice of veterans and military families and expressing gratitude for their role in defending the nation's freedoms. "Our veterans represent the very best of America: courage, selfishness, patriotism, and an unwavering commitment to something greater than themselves, Youngkin posted to X in part. Potential 2028 Democratic Contenders Several Democrats who posted Veterans Day messages are frequently mentioned as potential 2028 presidential contenders. Prediction markets and early political speculation have focused on figures including former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Georgia U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff and nearly a dozen others. Kamala Harris The former vice president and 2024 Democratic nominee has said she is "thinking about" a 2028 presidential campaign but has not decided. Harris sent a message on X Wednesday, thanking veterans and their families. "They represent the best of who we are as Americans," she wrote in part. Gavin Newsom The governor of California paired his Veterans Day tribute with a policy-focused message, arguing that honoring veterans requires providing housing, healthcare and economic opportunities for those who have served and their families. While Newsom has not announced a 2028 presidential campaign, he is widely viewed as a potential contender after years of building a national profile as one of the Democratic Party's most prominent voices. On X, in part, the governor honored "the extraordinary men and women who answered the call to serve our country." Josh Shapiro The Pennsylvania governor, also widely viewed as a potential Democratic presidential contender, has frequently appeared near the top of early 2028 polling and speculation about the party's future leadership. Shapiro marked Veterans Day with a personal tribute to his father, a Navy veteran, thanking him and other veterans for protecting American freedoms at home and abroad. "Nearly 700,000 veterans call Pennsylvania home — brave men and women who put on the uniform and served our Commonwealth and our country. On behalf of all of us, thank you for the countless sacrifices you made to fight for our freedoms and defend the values of our nation," the governor posted to X, in part. Pete Buttigieg The former transportation secretary, who previously sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020 and remains a frequent subject of 2028 speculation, has continued to appear in early polling and discussions about the party's next generation of national leaders. Buttigieg, a Navy Reserve veteran who deployed to Afghanistan, marked Veterans Day by honoring service members and veterans while reflecting on the sacrifices made by military families and those who have worn the uniform. "Without their courage, our way of life would be nothing but a pleasant theory," he said on X, in part. Jon Ossoff The U.S. senator from Georgia who won reelection last week also appears near the top of early 2028 polling on the Democratic Party's future leadership. "Veterans Day is not a day for sales at the mall. It's a day for us to reflect on our shared debt to those who have worn the uniform and served our nation and to their families," Ossoff said in a message shown on YouTube. "We are Americans first before we are Democrats or Republicans." Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Ocasio-Cortez, whose name has also regularly surfaced in speculation about the Democratic Party's future leadership, honored veterans and military families in a message marking their service and sacrifice. She says the government owes its veterans more. "This Veterans Day, we must move past words and pass legislation to guarantee robust benefits for all who have served," the New York Democrat posted to X, in part. news.title: 'Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it': Democrats react to Colom's win
news.text:
Democratic challenger Scott Colom's upset victory over Republican incumbent Hyde-Smith immediately drew reaction from prominent Democratic leaders across the country, who framed the result as both an historic breakthrough in Mississippi and one of the most significant victories of the 2026 midterm elections.

Colom's victory capped a campaign that transformed what was once considered a long-shot Democratic bid into one of the nation's most closely watched Senate contests.

A longtime district attorney, Scott Colom built his campaign around economic issues, government accountability and expanding opportunities in rural communities while drawing support from national Democratic figures, including former President Bill Clinton, who campaigned for him in the race's final days, the Mississippi Clarion Ledger, part of the USA TODAY Network, reported.

The contest attracted national attention as outside groups and party organizations poured millions of dollars into Mississippi, sensing an opportunity in a state Republicans had comfortably carried for decades.

The outcome was historic on multiple fronts. Colom became the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and the first Black Mississippian elected to the Senate since the Reconstruction era.

His victory over Hyde-Smith, who had served in the Senate since 2018, was widely described by national political observers as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 midterm elections and immediately fueled discussion about whether the result could signal broader shifts in Southern politics.

Bill Clinton: Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it

Clinton celebrated the outcome on X.

"We may have had to count One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, but Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it! Scott, you put your heart and soul into this race because you believe in the promise of your state's people. And they believed in you right back. I'm honored to have stood alongside you. Congratulations!"

The message echoed a broader sentiment among national Democrats who portrayed the result as evidence that Democrats can compete in states long considered safely Republican.

Chuck Schumer: 'Blue Mississippi Is Here'

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer quickly hailed the result, posting on X:

"Blue Mississippi is here. Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him."

Schumer's comments reflected the surprise and excitement among Democratic leaders after a victory few national analysts predicted when the campaign began.

Cory Booker highlights historic nature of win

For many Democrats, the election carried significance beyond party politics.

U.S. Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey emphasized Colom's place in history.

"Congratulations to my friend, Senator-elect Scott Colom. History was made today. You showed that hope rises in the South, and that Mississippi matters!"

Booker's remarks echoed a theme repeated throughout the day by Democratic officials and civil-rights advocates who pointed to Colom becoming Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

Bernie Sanders praises progressive message

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont focused on the substance of Colom's campaign, arguing voters responded to an anti-establishment economic message.

"Congratulations to Scott Colom on winning his election and making history as Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction.

Scott ran on a bold agenda — taking on Big Tech, the billionaire class and corruption in Washington — and WON.

Scott: Welcome to the Senate."

Sanders' endorsement of Colom's message added a progressive dimension to the national reaction surrounding the race.

Amy Klobuchar focuses on senate flip

U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota highlighted the electoral implications of the victory.

"Congratulations to Scott Colom on flipping Mississippi's Senate seat blue for the first time in nearly 40 years! What a great senator he will be!"

Her comments underscored how Democrats viewed the Mississippi result not simply as an individual victory but as the capture of a Senate seat that had been in Republican hands for decades.

Kamala Harris weighs in historic night

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who campaigned with Colom during the race, also celebrated the victory on X, writing that "the power is with the people, and the people of Mississippi are with Scott."

Harris called Colom's election "history" in the making, noting that he would become Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. She added that she had seen firsthand while campaigning with him in his hometown that he is "a brilliant leader," and said Mississippi voters had chosen a candidate who will fight for their future.

Mississippi Democrats join celebration

Reaction also poured in from Mississippi Democrats.

Former gubernatorial nominee Brandon Presley wrote:

"It is official, Mississippi has a new voice in Washington and it is Senator-Elect Scott Colom. Katelyn and I couldn't be happier for this beautiful family and our beloved Mississippi."

Gov. Tate Reeves wants to work with Colom

Even as national Democrats celebrated the upset, Gov. Tate Reeves struck a bipartisan tone in his public response. The Republican governor congratulated Scott Colom in a post on X and signaled a willingness to work with the senator-elect despite their political differences.

"Congratulations to Senator-Elect Scott Colom," Reeves wrote. "I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids."

Reeves' message reflected an emphasis on cooperation and governing priorities as Mississippi prepares to send a new senator to Washington.

Cindy Hyde-Smith Concedes

The outpouring of reaction came after Hyde-Smith formally conceded defeat, bringing an end to one of the nation's closest and most closely watched Senate races.

In a video posted to social media, Hyde-Smith said she accepted the outcome and congratulated her opponent.

"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

A result that resonated beyond Mississippi

The wave of reaction illustrated how quickly the race became a national political story. Democratic leaders celebrated a victory in a state President Trump carried comfortably two years earlier, while many focused on the historical significance of electing Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction and its first Democratic senator since 1982. National media outlets widely characterized the result as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 midterm election cycle.

Ross Reily is a writer for the Clarion Ledger, part of the USA TODAY Network. He can be reached at rreily@gannett.com. You can follow him on the X platform, formerly known as Twitter @GreenOkra1.

news.title: Another GOP defeat: Mississippi elects first Black senator since 1874
news.text: More than a week after the U.S. midterm elections delivered sweeping Democratic gains and cost Republicans control of both houses of Congress, Democrat Scott Colom has completed another extraordinary upset, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi. The victory gives Democrats their 55th Senate seat, compared with 44 for Republicans, with only the race in Alaska still unresolved. The result is particularly striking in Mississippi, one of the most reliably conservative states in the country. Democrats also scored breakthroughs in traditionally Republican territory elsewhere in the midterms, but Colom’s victory carries a distinction of its own: He is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis won reelection in 1982. Colom, 43, defeated Hyde-Smith, 67, who had served in the Senate since 2018. President Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. Colom also becomes Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era following the Civil War. Mississippi sent two Black Republicans to the Senate during Reconstruction: Hiram Revels, who served in 1870 and 1871, and Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery and was elected by the Mississippi Legislature in 1874 before serving a full Senate term from 1875 to 1881. The historical significance of Colom’s victory is amplified by Mississippi’s subsequent history of racial segregation and Black disenfranchisement under Jim Crow. During Reconstruction, the Ku Klux Klan also emerged as a violent white supremacist organization targeting Black Americans and their political rights. Among the symbolic results this year was Colom’s victory in Forrest County, a traditionally Republican county named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Klan’s first grand wizard. The Mississippi race remained undecided for more than a week as election officials processed absentee and provisional ballots. Colom finished election night with a lead of just 43 votes, but his advantage steadily expanded as counties completed their counts. The Associated Press called the race after his lead grew to more than 4,600 votes, a margin large enough that the remaining ballots were not expected to change the outcome. Hyde-Smith subsequently conceded. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer celebrated the result on X. “Blue Mississippi is here. Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him,” he wrote. “Scott will make a fantastic Senator for the people of Mississippi, and I can’t wait to welcome him to the Senate.” The only Senate contest still outstanding is Alaska. Democrats already hold a 55-44 advantage in the incoming 100-member Senate. A victory in Alaska would increase that majority to 56 seats, significant because most legislation subject to a filibuster requires 60 votes to end debate. The closer Democrats move to that threshold, the fewer Republican votes they would need to advance such measures. The upset forecasters missed and the protein ad behind it Unlike races in some other Republican strongholds that had attracted attention well before Election Day, Mississippi was not initially expected to become one of the country’s closest Senate contests. There were signs that Hyde-Smith was vulnerable and that voters were frustrated over the cost of living and high fuel prices, but the Cook Political Report rated the race “Solid Republican” until late October before shifting it to “Likely Republican.” Trump’s commanding 2024 performance reinforced those assumptions. But Colom spent months insisting that the political environment in Mississippi was changing and urging national Democrats to invest more heavily in his campaign. He argued that unusually strong Black turnout, combined with dissatisfaction over prices and the Trump administration, could make the race competitive. Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi’s population. The morning after Election Day, while much of the country was still surprised by the razor-thin result, Colom said his campaign had expected exactly that kind of race. “Unlike all the people across the country that might be surprised, our campaign, our volunteers, the people of Mississippi are not surprised,” he said. His team had prepared lawyers and volunteers across the state to monitor the remaining count. Colom’s fundraising accelerated late in the campaign, and prominent Democrats including former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Bill Clinton traveled to Mississippi to support him. But much of his campaign remained intensely local, centered on town halls, grassroots organizing and appeals to voters who had traditionally supported Republicans. His central themes were the cost of living, health care and high gasoline and grocery prices. Hyde-Smith inadvertently provided Colom with one of his most effective campaign messages. Asked in a local television interview about rising beef prices, she responded, “You have so many proteins to choose from.” Colom’s campaign turned the remark into a viral advertisement featuring Mississippi voters reacting incredulously to the suggestion. One man grilling hamburgers told the camera: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The ad drew millions of views and became shorthand for Colom’s argument that Hyde-Smith was disconnected from the economic pressures facing ordinary residents. He continued the joke on the campaign trail, including appearances involving food trucks offering voters different protein choices. Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, a father of two and a practicing Christian who made his faith and family history central parts of his campaign. His mother, Dorothy Colom, broke racial barriers when she was elected a chancery court judge, while his father, Wilbur Colom, was a prominent attorney and longtime Republican who worked for Ronald Reagan. Before running for the Senate, Colom had already made history in Mississippi politics. He served as a judge and prosecutor before winning election in 2015 as district attorney for the state’s 16th Judicial District, becoming the first Black person elected to the post. He built his Senate campaign around the argument that he could attract both the state’s large Black electorate and moderate or traditionally Republican voters. His victory now places him in a political lineage stretching directly back to Reconstruction. Colom has said the significance of becoming Mississippi’s first Black senator in generations also carries a responsibility to ensure that he is not the last, and that his performance in office should make it easier rather than harder for future candidates from similar backgrounds to succeed. The election also carries an element of personal political reversal. President Joe Biden nominated Colom in 2022 to become a federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith refused to return the Senate Judiciary Committee’s required “blue slip,” preventing it from advancing. Hyde-Smith later boasted about blocking the nomination. “He thought he was going to be a federal judge, and I blocked him,” she said during her reelection campaign. Colom has denied that his Senate run was motivated by revenge, instead emphasizing affordability, health care and government accountability. Now, the man Hyde-Smith prevented from reaching the federal bench will replace her in the U.S. Senate. As Colom put it while the ballots were still being counted: “The bottom line is this is the beginning of a new direction for our state.”
news.summary: Nine days after Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, Scott Colom ousts Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in deep-red Mississippi, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and giving Democrats their 55th Senate seat

news.title: Uncut footage exposes Trump’s ‘rigged’ rambling scrubbed by Bari Weiss’ network: analyst
news.text:
Viewers of President Donald Trump's latest network interview missed much of what he said, and a progressive political analyst says that helped him.

David Pakman said on Wednesday's episode of "The David Pakman Show" that CBS News' "60 Minutes" cut about half of its recorded interview with the president, including Trump's insistence that the 2020 election was "rigged." The edits, Pakman argued, made Trump "look a lot less crazy, even though he still looked nuts in the interview."

The interview, which aired Sunday, was conducted by Ross Douthat, a conservative New York Times columnist who Pakman noted joined CBS under Bari Weiss, the network's editor in chief. Pakman said the broadcast segment ran about 27 minutes with narration and transitions included, while the full recording ran about 52 minutes.

Pakman walked through a side-by-side edit from Decoding Fox News that shows the aired footage in color and the removed footage in black and white. In one exchange, Trump answered a question about the biggest obstacle to peace in Ukraine by pointing to the "hatred" between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. What viewers didn't see, Pakman said, was Trump drifting from there into his 2020 election grievances.

"They are making Trump look less unhinged and more coherent by removing that," Pakman said.

He added that the network also cut Trump's rambling about an upcoming meeting and trimmed an exchange about arming Ukraine in which Trump made "wacky claims" about former President Barack Obama.

"What they broadcast on TV was this tight answer that makes it seem as though Trump is staying on topic when he isn't, and this happened throughout the interview," Pakman said.

The analyst acknowledged that "60 Minutes" routinely edits interviews and that he doesn't know the reason behind every cut, noting some may have been requested by Trump's camp.

"But the effect of these edits is Trump doesn't seem like he's rambling as much. Trump doesn't seem like he's lying as much," he said.

Pakman contrasted the edits with Trump's lawsuit over the network's October 2024 interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, which Trump branded election interference. Trump also suggested CBS should lose its broadcast license. Pakman noted Paramount settled in July 2025 for $16 million without admitting wrongdoing while it sought federal approval for its merger with Skydance.

As part of that settlement, Pakman said, Paramount agreed to release transcripts of future presidential candidate interviews, and CBS posted the extended Trump interview on YouTube.

"It wasn't hidden," Pakman said. "But we now see damn Trump really benefited from the edit."

He then turned the president's own argument back on him.

"So if editing an interview is election interference, when CBS does it to Kamala Harris, what is it when they do it to Trump's interview?" Pakman asked. "Funny how that works, isn't it?"

news.title: Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race in major victory for Democrats
news.text:
In perhaps the most stunning upset of the 2026 midterm cycle, Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s closely contested Senate race.

Colom’s historic win marks the eighth Senate seat that Democrats were able to flip from Republican control this cycle, giving the party a total of 55 seats in the chamber. If Democrats win the still-undecided Alaska Senate race, their majority will grow to 56-44.

Hyde-Smith called Colom to concede around 6 p.m. ET, two sources close to the Colom campaign told MS NOW. The GOP senator posted a video to X moments later, saying, “I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Colom will become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the Southern GOP stronghold since 1982. His surprise victory underscores the seismic shift toward the Democratic Party, even in the Deep South.

Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP, hailed the victory for Colom, and for Black voters whose political power was curtailed by the Supreme Court and threatened by the Trump administration.

“Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy,” Johnson said. "Even in the face of efforts to remove voters from the rolls, attempts to intimidate voters and election officials, and bids to create fear around the electoral process, Mississippi voters showed up.”

The Associated Press declared Colom the winner on Wednesday evening, after his hairline lead steadily grew during the state’s protracted counting of thousands of mail-in-absentee and provisional ballots, which are known in the state as affidavit ballots. 

The latest vote tally update proved decisive: Jackson County, a Republican stronghold, reported more than 2,000 additional votes, but Hyde-Smith failed to gain any ground on her opponent. By Wednesday, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by 4,669 votes, a margin too wide for the Republican incumbent to close.

The race between Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, and Hyde-Smith, a Trump loyalist who voted against certifying the results of the 2020 presidential election, became the nail-biter of the midterms. Ironically, the Democratic challenger had Hyde-Smith to thank for his own candidacy.

Colom was nominated to be a federal judge by former President Joe Biden in 2023, but Hyde-Smith single-handedly blocked his nomination — paving the way for him to run against her, and win, three years later.

Because Mississippi is the only state in the country without a recount law, lawyers for both campaigns had descended on the state the day after Election Day as Republicans prepared for a potential legal challenge.

Colom campaigned relentlessly to become the state’s first Democratic senator in nearly 45 years. Democrat Scott Colom will upset Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, The Associated Press projected Wednesday, flipping a Republican seat in a ruby-red state.

He also went viral with a campaign video where he mocked Hyde-Smith over comments she made about choosing other options for proteins because of high beef prices.

news.title: Mississippi didn’t flip. Mississippians flipped it.
news.text:
I tried to tell you all. In January, I said on “The Weeknight” that Scott Colom could be a convincing candidate for the U.S. Senate. In August, when our list of 12 Senate races to watch left Mississippi off, I told viewers to pay attention anyway. I believed he could win.

Wednesday night, it became official: Colom defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Black senator elected by Mississippi voters and the first Democrat the state has sent to the Senate since 1982. The last Black senators chosen to represent Mississippi, Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce, were selected during Reconstruction, a time when all U.S. senators were picked by state legislators and not voters.

In 1962, Fannie Lou Hamer went to the courthouse in Indianola to try to register to vote. The plantation owner she worked for told her to withdraw her application. She refused and lost her job. Two years later, she went to the Democratic National Convention to challenge an all-white delegation that claimed to represent Mississippi. Hamer understood that representation depended on who had the power to choose and that building that power took work.

People keep asking me what I saw in this race.

People keep asking me what I saw in this race. I saw a candidate who knew how to compete in Mississippi, and years of nonpartisan organizing that helped build an electorate ready to hear him.

Start with Colom himself. He had already won election as district attorney in a majority-white district and been re-elected twice. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship. Mississippi’s senior Republican senator, Roger Wicker, supported the nomination. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith used the Senate’s “blue slip” tradition to block it. This year, Colom asked Mississippians to send him to the Senate in her place. 

When I asked Colom in July how he intended to win, he told me he was going after young people, people who had given up on politics and people who had voted Republican before. I took him seriously because he understood what it would take to get those people to hear him out. He held five town halls in five days. He went to Corinth and talked to people waiting in line to see President Donald Trump rally for his opponent.

When Colom came back on our show in October, he was still talking about what people were paying for groceries, gas and healthcare. When he talked about Medicaid and hospitals in the Delta, he was talking about whether people would be able to get care close to home. That was the campaign he ran. It gave people who might never have considered voting for him a reason to listen, and it gave people who were ready for a change a reason to turn out.

In August, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks became the first senator to campaign with him in Mississippi. As the campaign went on, Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester, Cory Booker and Raphael Warnock, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and former Vice President Kamala Harris followed.

But the people of Mississippi believed first.

After Hurricane Katrina, Derrick Johnson, now president of the NAACP, founded One Voice, a Jackson-based nonprofit that trains Black Mississippians in civic engagement. It brought local leaders together and helped develop new ones. After Democrats lost the state House in 2011, Mississippi organizers kept building. Local groups used voter data to run their own canvassing operations and stay in touch with people between elections. They had their own relationships and their own reasons to knock on those doors. 

In DeSoto County in 2019, Hester Jackson-McCray went looking for people who had just moved into her district and hadn’t registered, then went back to make sure they had turned in their paperwork. She became the first Black person to represent DeSoto County in the legislature. Some of that was nonpartisan organizing, and some was candidates like her doing it themselves. All of it was happening long before the national party had a Senate race to put money into.

When I said in March that Mississippi was no accident, I was thinking about two races for the state Senate. The Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP and Black voters had gone to court over maps that diluted Black voting strength. Under court-ordered maps, voters elected Theresa Gillespie Isom and Johnny DuPree. With those two seats, Republicans lost their supermajority. That was one reason I took Colom’s chances seriously. People in Mississippi had already fought for a fairer chance to choose who represented them, and when they got that chance, they used it.

Give the Democratic National Committee credit. It made a six-figure investment in the Mississippi Democratic Party’s organizing ahead of those 2025 special elections. I wish the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had shown that same confidence in this race. The DSCC announced a $500,000 coordinated ad buy only six days before Election Day.

Imagine celebrating the power of Black voters in Mississippi, then leaving them to defend it on their own.

Colom is going to Washington. The people who sent him there are still fighting over who gets to represent them at home. In May the Supreme Court set aside the ruling that produced those state Senate maps. Lawmakers have already held redistricting hearings, candidates start qualifying in January, and some Republicans are talking about carving up the majority-Black congressional district represented by Bennie Thompson, the only Black member of Mississippi’s U.S. House delegation. Imagine celebrating the power of Black voters in Mississippi this week, then leaving them to defend it on their own next week.

Next year, Mississippians will elect a new governor and members of both chambers of the Legislature. The national party and the outside groups that showed up in October have all the evidence they need. Put money behind the plans local organizations are already making for 2027, and give those organizations a permanent say in how it’s spent. If Mississippi Republicans can see enough power in these communities to want to divide them, national Democrats ought to see enough to invest in them.

But this was never the party’s story. It belongs to the young people Mississippi Votes brought into this election, many of them voting for the first time. It belongs to the Black women who have carried organizing in this state for generations, and to the canvassers who kept knocking on doors in the years when there was no Senate race to knock for. 

In 1964, Fannie Lou Hamer stood before the Democratic National Convention’s credentials committee and asked the country, “Is this America?” Sixty-two years later, Mississippians are still answering her. They didn’t wait for anyone to believe in them. 

They believed first, and the rest of us are still catching up.

news.title: How Scott Colom won deep-red Mississippi with little help from Democrats
news.text:
The ad is simple, less than half a minute long, but many say it was the moment the nation took notice of Mississippi’s US Senate race.

In it, the incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer, answers a reporter’s question about the rising price of beef: “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she says.

The ad then cuts to a man flipping burgers on a grill. “Pick another protein?” he says. “Shhiiiiii – I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

The viral ad was for Hyde-Smith’s Democratic challenger, Scott Colom, who won the Senate seat on Wednesday, becoming the first Democratic senator in Mississippi since 1982 and its first Black senator since the Reconstruction era. His ads were relevant to Mississippians and created memorable slogans – an early ad highlighted the history and progress of the state, while a more recent one spoofed the hit film Sinners, filmed in Mississippi. But his efforts to engage Mississippians didn’t start there.

Colom spent the past year reaching Mississippi residents where they were. From driving a “pick another protein” truck that offered free tacos, to talking to students and alums at college homecomings, to chatting with voters queued to see Donald Trump, Colom campaigned on an idea that’s not novel to Mississippians, but one that the rest of the country is only starting to fully realize: “Mississippi Matters.”

And he did it with little help from the Democratic party.

‘We’re a state that has to matter’

When Colom announced his campaign last year, pundits largely wrote him off as another Democratic challenger with no chance of winning. For much of the campaign cycle, prognosticators labeled the Senate seat as “solid R”, something he said made it more difficult for him to fundraise.

Within three months of launching his campaign, Colom raised about $594,000. In that same period, Hyde-Smith raised nearly $1.1m, including a significant donation from Aipac, the pro-Israel lobbying group. Shortly before the election, Colom had raised about $3.6m, compared with Hyde-Smith’s $5.3m. It’s also hard to unseat an incumbent senator in Mississippi – prior to Colom’s election, it hadn’t been done since 1942.

But this wasn’t Colom’s first uphill battle.

In 2015, he unseated an incumbent who’d held the circuit’s district attorney’s seat for almost three decades. That election made Colom the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit, a position in which he held a 94% success rate for convictions.

In 2023, Biden nominated Colom, a seventh-generation Mississippian, to serve as a US district court judge for the northern district of Mississippi. Republicans, including the senator Roger Wicker, and Democrats alike supported the nomination. But Hyde-Smith blocked it.

On election day, well before the race was called, Hyde-Smith joked about her decision, saying: “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a US Senator.”

In the end, Mississippi didn’t block Colom. He knew that to win, he needed Black voter turnout and the support of about a quarter of white voters. And that’s what he did, flipping counties that had been Republican strongholds.

Part of Colom’s campaign success was his ability to talk to voters as people, two Mississippians having a chat, not as someone trying to solicit a vote.

“I don’t do speeches,” Colom said days before the election. “I speak from my heart. I talk about what I care about, I listen to people.”

He talked to people at Waffle Houses, chatted them up in barber shops and hair salons, and visited with employees at fast food restaurants and big box stores.

By April, the senator Ralph Warnock was telling national Democrats to pay attention to Colom’s campaign. Instead, they laughed at him. It wasn’t until a month before the election – seeing the impact of “pick another protein” and Colom’s rising popularity outside the state – that the party began seriously infusing cash into the campaign. National leaders such as Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg and Cory Booker stumped across the Magnolia state. Colom’s momentum, which had steadily been building for months, crescendoed even more.

“[People have to] understand how much potential and promise we have in Mississippi,” he said. “We’re a state that has to matter, that this country will never reach its potential if it ignores places like Mississippi.”

‘I speak from my heart’

Colom and Hyde-Smith spent the week after the election much differently. Despite Colom maintaining a lead of several thousand votes over Hyde-Smith, the incumbent senator refused to concede. Historic voter turnout, combined with data inaccurately marking voters inactive, left all 82 counties in the state having to count affidavit ballots, a process that took days.

While Hyde-Smith didn’t appear during that time, Colom did. He used the national media attention that he was receiving to highlight local people and businesses.

“I’m glad that the media is getting an opportunity to see our state,” he told reporters. “Go out to talk to some Mississippians – they’re very proud of this moment.” He encouraged journalists to go to local museums and shouted out colleges.

He also used that time to thank voters.

The day after the election, Colom visited Millsaps College, his alma mater, and Tougaloo College, a historically Black college whose students have been active in the fight for voting rights.

At Millsaps, Colom walked out to raucous cheers from the students who gathered on campus to see him. He focused little on the campaign, instead talking to students about his time at Millsaps and the value of an education. The visit also gave him a chance to thank the professor who gave him the confidence to run for office. Colom attended Millsaps to play basketball, but Anne MacMaster, an English professor, asked him to read a passage from Richard Wright, the Mississippi author of the landmark novel Native Son, when he was a sophomore.

“That is the most beautiful reading of Richard Wright I’ve ever heard,” Colom recalled her saying. “You can only read that as a Mississippian that’s understood what those words actually mean.”

MacMaster eventually became his adviser and the reason he double-majored in history and English. Colom, who, days later, would become the next senator from Mississippi, hugged MacMaster. But their interaction had to be brief.

There was a swarm of people, eager to talk to Colom one-on-one.

news.title: Democrat Scott Colom elected as Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction
news.text: Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South. The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term. “They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch. Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society. “It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don’t come up with excuses as to why we can’t do it,” he said. The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy. The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized. Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.” When Trump went to Corinth, Miss., in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities. Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?” Then she stepped away. “I love that,” Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. “Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes.” The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi. There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination. Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith. The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family. “In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.” Black Democrats, including Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, highlighted Colom's bid early. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate. Former President Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks. With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points. Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi. Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points. Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction. During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story. “My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.” Barrow and Bates write for the Associated Press.
news.summary: Mississippi has elected its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction and delivered Democrats a major upset in a rocky midterm election for the GOP.

news.title: Dem Scott Colom defeats Mississippi Sen. Hyde-Smith after weeklong nailbiter
news.text:
Democrat Scott Colom upset Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the tightly contested Mississippi Senate election after more than a week of vote counting.

Colom garnered 49.2% of the vote, compared to Hyde-Smith’s (R-Miss.) 48.7%, with more than 95% of the ballots tallied Wednesday.The naillbiter race — the two candidates were separated by less than 5,000 votes — was called by multiple outlets more than week after Election Day. 

Colom, the district attorney for Mississippi’s 16th Judicial District, becomes the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the Magnolia State since John Stennis in 1982.Hyde-Smith, who was first appointed to the Senate in 2018, had won her 2020 race by a comfortable 10 point margin. 

President Trump was in Mississippi as part of his midterm blitz in the run-up to Election Day — a desperate bid to shore up support in ruby red Republican strongholds.

It was a state that he won by 22.9% in 2024 — up 6.4 percentage points from his 2020 performance in the state — but polls blared warning signs for the Republicans, forcing Trump to campaign with Hyde-Smith.Colom, meanwhile, was boosted by former President Bill Clinton, ex-Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, all of whom stumped for the Democratic DA on the campaign trail.

The Democrats racked up a string of shock wins in red states– including Iowa, Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas — in a massive rebuke of Trump and the GOP government in Washington.

news.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
news.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

After more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee ballots and affidavit — or provisional — ballots, Colom won the closest Senate race in the country by just a few thousand votes.

In a midterm full of stunning upsets for Democrats, Colom's victory underscores a dramatic shift in the political landscape across the South driven by a surge of Black voter turnout.

Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%, but President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years and hasn't sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction. 

The state's rural, agriculture-heavy economy was disproportionately impacted by rising prices, and saw millions in investment from both parties, particularly in the final weeks of the race. Colom, a district attorney, made cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign message, decrying "Cindy High-Prices" as bad for Mississippi.

Unlike most other contested Senate races that flipped, Mississippi did not see much national money or attention until the closing days of the election. That included a rally in the final week by President Trump and high-profile visits from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and other Democrats. The Cook Political Report had the race rated as Likely Republican going into election night.

Colom told NPR earlier this month that a lack of investment from national Democrats until the last minute was a mistake.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."

Colom's campaign was a contrast in style from Hyde-Smith, who rarely spoke to reporters in Washington and had minimal presence in the state.

When asked about high beef prices earlier this year, Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and onetime state agriculture commissioner — said that "you have so many other proteins to choose from."

That led to a viral campaign ad from Colom, which featured several people expressing disbelief at the senator's suggestion to "pick another protein." Instead, the ad said, it was time to "pick another senator."
news.summary: Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate in Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

news.title: Mississippi, Once the Epicenter of Jim Crow, Elects Its First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
news.text:
For the closing ad of his US Senate campaign, Democrat Scott Colom stood in the driveway of the house that once belonged to Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who was assassinated by a white supremacist in 1963 while holding T-shirts that said “Jim Crow Must Go.”

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” said Colom. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.” 

Now Colom, in a fitting tribute to Evers, has made history as the first Black US senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. The longtime district attorney is also the first Black candidate to win any statewide office in Mississippi since Reconstruction.

His shocking upset victory in a state where Donald Trump won by 23 points in 2024 is even more remarkable considering Mississippi’s history.

This was the state where Jim Crow was the most violent and repressive. It was where Emmett Till was lynched, Evers was assassinated, and the young civil rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan. There were 581 documented lynchings during the Jim Crow era, more than any other state.

“Just to mention Mississippi, to cross the state line from Alabama and go there, it just created all types of problems in my own mind,” the late congressman and civil rights activist John Lewis once said. “It seemed like when you just drove over the state line, something happened to the air, to the environment. It was a psychological thing… Alabama is bad; Alabama is hell. But to go to Mississippi at the time was worse than hell.”

Before the passage of the Voting Rights Act, only 6.7 percent of eligible Black voters were registered to vote in Mississippi.

Now, more than 60 years later, it was Black voters who turned out in record numbers to rewrite the history books, motivated in part by a new struggle to protect voting rights. 

As was the case across the South, the Supreme Court’s demolition of the Voting Rights Act in the Louisiana v. Callais decision spurred Black voters to cast their ballots at a historic rate. Following the decision, Mississippi Republican Gov. Tate Reeves called on the legislature to pass a new map sometime before 2027 that would oust Rep. Bennie Thompson, the only Black member of Congress from the state. Thompson earned national prominence as chair of the US House committee investigating the January 6 attacks. Echoing the racist rhetoric white segregationists used to attack Black voting power during Reconstruction, Reeves announced that Thompson’s “reign of terror” would soon be over. 

After Reeves’ announcement, thousands of civil rights supporters, including Colom, rallied in Jackson in protest. It was the largest mass demonstration in the state since the civil rights era. “That was an incredible example of the level of anger and frustration and energy that exists here in Mississippi and across the South in response to the Callais decision,” says Amir Badat, a Mississippi native who serves as the Southern states director for Fair Fight Action, the voting rights group founded by Stacey Abrams. “All of the energy that we saw among Mississippians, in particular among Black Mississippians, fed directly into the turnout that we saw for this election…People were able to make that direct connection between maps and the issues that affect them on a day-to-day basis.”

Colom turned the impending loss of Black representation—in the state with the largest percentage of Black people in the country—into a rallying cry on the campaign trail.

“They want to try to go back where our vote and our voice doesn’t matter,” he said. “And thank god our ancestors gave us the one power we need in this moment…the power to vote.”

The Black share of the electorate increased by three points in Mississippi from 2024 to 2026—enough to make the difference for Colom in a race decided by just a few thousand votes. According to exit polling by CNN, Colom won 27 percent of the white vote but 97 percent of the Black vote. In majority-Black counties in Mississippi, turnout reached 87.4 percent of 2024 levels compared to 73.8 percent in majority-white counties, the largest gap in the South, according to data compiled by Tom Bonier, a senior adviser with the Democratic data firm TargetSmart. In recent elections, Black turnout lagged behind white turnout in the South—in 2026, that trend was reversed.

Mississippi voters cited “democracy” as their second most important issue in the campaign, after the economy, and those voters broke for Colom by a 2–1 margin.

“Black voters recognized that the 2026 midterm election quite literally was an existential moment for our democracy,” says Charles Taylor, executive director of the Mississippi NAACP. “So you saw that play out where now we have made history 150 years in the making.”

Even before the Callais decision, Taylor commissioned a poll during Mississippi’s primary in March asking Black voters if they’d rather have a candidate prioritize protecting their rights or lowering costs. Three-quarters said protecting their rights.

Taylor said the Mississippi NAACP raised four times as much money this year compared to previous election cycles, allowing them to make an “absolutely unprecedented” investment in organizing that included opening 11 voter registration field offices, registering more than 17,000 new voters, knocking on 150,000 doors in 40 counties, sending 700,000 mailers, and 1.4 million text messages. “We told people that we needed them to vote,” Taylor said, “and Scott did a great job convincing them that he was the one to vote for.”

Colom’s campaign had to overcome the state’s many demons from the past while inspiring a new way forward that embraced, rather than rejected, multiracial democracy. He won Hinds County, where Evers lived, by 61 points. He won Sunflower County, the home of notorious segregationist former Senator James Eastland, by 52 points. He won Leflore County, where Till was lynched, by 51 points. He flipped Forrest County, named after KKK founder Nathan Bedford Forrest. He lost Neshoba County, where Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner were murdered, but improved upon Kamala Harris’ numbers by 28 points. 

And Colom had to fight a persistent system of voter suppression that seems designed to preserve the white power structure. Mississippi ranked dead last in the country in voter turnout during the last midterm and at the bottom of ease of voting. It has no early voting, no online registration, and voters must have a government-approved reason to cast an absentee ballot. On top of that, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson removed 1 in 9 voters from the rolls in the run-up to the election based on faulty credit data, forcing many otherwise eligible voters to cast provisional ballots that may—or may not—have been counted. “One big takeaway from this is that the system in Mississippi is broken in many ways,” says Badat. 

In the end, Colom was a joyful warrior, playfully skewering his GOP opponent Cindy Hyde-Smith for suggesting that Mississippians should “pick another protein” because of the price of beef and casting her as a vampire in a viral Halloween parody of Sinners called “Sinators” that featured his twin brother. It was Hyde-Smith who blocked Colom from becoming a federal judge during the Biden administration, but he finally got his revenge. Sometimes the weight of history is so heavy in Mississippi that it’s better to laugh than cry.

Colom’s election will have immediate ramifications on the politics of Mississippi. Leading Republicans expected the governor to call a special session after the election to redraw Mississippi’s congressional and legislative maps. That has not happened yet. “If I were the Republicans in the legislature or in the state government and I were thinking about whether or not to redistrict, I would would take a really hard look at the results that we saw in this election because it’s going to make it way harder for them to eliminate Black-majority districts and still feel safe that their Republican incumbents are going to be able to win,” says Badat.

The elimination of Bennie Thompson’s district and majority-Black seats in the legislature would likely motivate Black voters to turn out in higher numbers again for state elections next year, when legislative and statewide elections take place. “I think the significance of this victory is that now people in Mississippi understand that they can exercise their power to achieve real change, and I think that’s going to translate into engagement for the 2027 elections as well,” Badat adds. 

Colom’s improbable win is much bigger than simply a political victory. Angela Grayson, civic engagement director of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, a nonprofit pro-democracy group, cited the impact it will have on her two daughters in college. “What it means for me is an opportunity for them to be able to come home and want to stay and be able to not just live in Mississippi and survive, but then be able to thrive,” she says. “What I want for them more than anything is to have representation at every level. Someone in government who understands their lived experiences, and then be advocating for a better quality of life for them.”

The fight for civil rights is not ancient history for many in Mississippi, including Taylor. He sees Colom’s election as “a dawn of a new day in the state.”

Taylor is the seventh executive director of the Mississippi NAACP. The first was Medgar Evers. “His office is my office, and that’s a weird thing to say, and I say it very humbly,” Taylor says. Every window in the building is lined with bullet holes. He thought about the significance of that when he saw Colom’s closing ad. “After watching that ad I took a moment and just reflected on all of what has transpired over the last 60-plus years.”

Today, Mississippi has more Black elected officials than any other state. When Evers was alive that number was zero.

“Medgar Evers did the work that we did this year,” Taylor says, “which was take a piece of paper and ask someone to put their name on it in order to be one step closer to exercising the most fundamental promise of our democracy.”
