news.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
news.text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.

Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.

The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom’s favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.

A spokesman for Hyde-Smith confirmed that she has called Colom to concede.

The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.

“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.

Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

“It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don’t come up with excuses as to why we can’t do it,” he said.

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer celebrated on social media.

“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done,” Schumer wrote. “Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South.”

A race Washington once viewed as a longshot

Despite Schumer’s support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom’s candidacy well after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, urged donors and party leaders to see the contest as winnable.

The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith’s vulnerabilities crystallized.

Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”

When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.

Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”

Then she stepped away.

“I love that,” Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. “Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes.”

The appearance tracked Colom’s tactic of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.

There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.

Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state.

Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.

Colom called on Mississippi’s history

The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.

“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said, telling the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

Black Democrats, including Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, highlighted Colom’s bid early. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.

Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom’s behalf in the campaign’s closing weeks.

Despite Republicans’ domination, the path was always there

With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.

Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.

Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.

Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.

During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.

“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”

news.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race, breaking the GOP’s grip on the state
news.text: In a major upset, Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, NBC News projects, capping off a string of Democratic victories by flipping the reddest seat yet in this year’s midterms. Mississippi last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago, just a few weeks before Colom was born in 1982. Colom will become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The historic win comes after days of uncertainty in the race, with Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith as more votes continued to be counted. Colom, a district attorney, remained confident throughout the vote counting that he would prevail. Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video message Wednesday evening. “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.” Colom is expected to address his supporters at a victory party later Wednesday night. Colom’s campaign confirmed to NBC News that Hyde-Smith had called him to concede. Colom’s victory means Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats next year. The only Senate race left to be called is in Alaska. In the next Congress, no Democratic senator will represent a redder state than Colom. Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024. Colom’s victory also underscores the Trump administration’s broad unpopularity with voters just two years after that presidential election, even in parts of the ruby-red Deep South. A majority of Mississippi voters said they disapproved of Trump’s overall job performance, according to NBC News exit polling. Majorities also said that his policies, including tariffs, hurt the economy and that it was wrong for the U.S. to take military action in Iran. Colom, the eighth Democrat to flip a Republican-held Senate seat so far this year, long believed Democrats had an opportunity to win Mississippi, given its sizable Black population and plenty of white voters in rural areas who he thought could back a Democrat. He chided his party for writing off the state. “We were never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause,” Colom recently told NBC News. “We were betrayed by Cindy Hyde-Smith because she allowed tariffs to hurt us. She allowed people — hundreds of thousands of Mississippians — to lose healthcare. She gave away our voice in the war in Iran, which drove up costs for farmers and for truckers and for businesses.” “But for too long we were also a betrayed cause by the national party, because they did not compete in this state,” Colom added. In late October, the Senate Majority PAC, a top Democratic super PAC, announced an ad campaign in the state through Election Day, starting with a 30-second spot that presented Colom as a crusader who would “fight corruption in both parties.” The group ended up spending nearly $2.1 million on the airwaves, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. The GOP super PAC Senate Leadership Fund responded with a similar-sized buy, airing ads that painted Colom as “too liberal” and “too radical.” The race also drew high-profile surrogates from both parties. Trump traveled to Mississippi eight days before the election, while Democrats such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia hit the campaign trail for Colom. Former President Barack Obama also appeared in an ad that the Colom campaign launched on digital platforms. Republicans tried to leverage those surrogates against Colom, with the Senate Leadership Fund launching one ad with a narrator saying, “Colom proudly campaigns with Kamala Harris because Colom supports their radical agenda.” But it was not enough to defeat Colom, who sharply criticized Hyde-Smith’s vote for Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which cut Medicaid funds. Colom also faulted Hyde-Smith’s support for the Trump administration’s tariff regime and the costly war with Iran, labeling his opponent “Cindy High Prices.” Colom’s campaign also created a viral video highlighting Hyde-Smith’s comments that Mississippians struggling with high beef prices “have so many proteins to choose from.” The video featured clips of people saying: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator.” Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner who was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and won a full term in 2020, campaigned as a reliable conservative and tried to portray Colom as a “radical” progressive. She also touted her loyalty to Trump, who endorsed her more than a year before the midterms and said she was “100% MAGA.” Hyde-Smith said that over the last week, her campaign team “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.” “I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: An election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will,” she said. Colom and Hyde-Smith had crossed paths before this year’s midterm elections. She blocked his nomination for a federal judgeship during the Biden administration. Colom recently told NBC News that he had forgiven her.

news.title: Less than half of Americans 'looking forward to' 2028 election: poll
news.text:
With the midterm elections behind us, a recent CNN/SSRS poll shows less than half of Americans are looking forward to the upcoming 2028 presidential election.

In the poll conducted about a month before the midterms, 40% of respondents said they were “looking forward to” the 2028 presidential contest, while another 27% said they were “dreading” it and 33% said they were “neither” looking forward to nor dreading the race.

Beyond their general feelings about the 2028 presidential contest, 64% of Americans said they did not have a specific person in mind for 2028; as of Nov. 11, no major candidates have declared their intention to run.

The 2028 presidential election will be quite different for an entire generation of Americans, as it will be the first without President Donald Trump’s name on the ballot in more than a decade; the 22nd Amendment bars him from serving another term in the White House.

The poll, conducted Oct. 15-18, surveyed 1,701 respondents with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

Voters show excitement for some candidates

According to CNN/SSRS, about a quarter of Democrat and Democratic-leaning Independent voters said they would be excited to support former Vice President Kamala Harris (27%), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (27%) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (26%) if they decided to run for president in 2028.

Behind them, Democratic-leaning voters advocated for California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, both at 22%.

Among Republicans and Republican-leaning Independents, two potential candidates were far and away the ones who voters were excited to support, with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both at 41%.

In third was Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (23%), with Texas Sen. Ted Cruz in fourth (15%).

Trump begins to step back

With Trump off the ballot, the president now says he may step away from the GOP’s presidential primary and not endorse a potential successor.

"We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with," Trump said in a Nov. 8 interview on CBS, pointing to Rubio as being "great" in addition to Vance. "But there are many others, and I'd rather not mention their names. There's some senators that are excellent. I know them all. I like them a lot."

"So I may or may not get involved," Trump said. "Maybe I'm better off not getting involved."

USA TODAY’s Joey Garrison contributed to this report.

news.title: Biden says he wouldn't have run for a second term in 2024 if he knew he had cancer
news.text:
ATLANTA — Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.

The former Democratic president’s comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.

“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer,” said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, “I would’ve not gone forward” with a 2024 reelection bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.

Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.

“I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running” for president, Biden said in the interview.

Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than five months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats’ concerns about his age — he was 81 at the time — and his ability to defeat Trump.

“First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t,” Biden said. “But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”

Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election.

Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.

“I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job,” he said.

His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects,” he said.

Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation’s direction and launching his own cryptocurrency.

Joe Biden defended his son’s public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden’s 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges. Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings.

Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father’s legacy, but the former president said Trump’s penchant for vengeance made it necessary.

“He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do,” Joe Biden said. “If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me — he would go back and try to do harm to them.”

Biden called his son “one of the brightest men I know,” adding, “I’m really proud of him.”
news.summary: ATLANTA — Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.

news.title: Trumpworld Insider Reveals Barrage of GOP Texts Bashing Vance
news.text:
Even Republican operatives aren’t feeling optimistic about JD Vance’s 2028 odds, a top political correspondent has revealed.

Mark Halperin said dozens of GOP strategists and operatives have shared negative views of the vice president in the embarrassing aftermath of the blue tsunami that saw Democrats wrest control of Congress from Republicans.

“I’ve been struck by the negativity about JD Vance,” Halperin said on the 2WAY podcast The Morning Meeting. “I’ve talked now to 68 people, mostly Republican strategists, operatives, et cetera. And the negativity about the vice president is quite something [for] someone who I thought, up to two weeks ago, was the obvious frontrunner.”

Halperin has been speaking with political operatives ahead of the release of his “8 for ‘28” power rankings. 

His list of potential Democratic frontrunners ranks Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. The bottom half is occupied by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, and Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly.

Halperin’s list for the GOP, meanwhile, comes out Thursday.

“In doing this reporting, again, with really serious Republican sources—some grassroots, some establishment—again, I’ve been struck by how negative they are about the vice president,” he said.

But that doesn’t mean Vance isn’t still viewed as a frontrunner in MAGAworld.

“However, I will tell you, previewing what I’m publishing tomorrow, he is number one on my list,” Halperin said.

The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After Republicans suffered humiliating losses in the midterms, Vance released a lengthy statement blaming the results on Americans’ dissatisfaction with the Iran war and the skyrocketing cost of living.

“I remain hopeful about our country,” he concluded. “To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.”

Mark Halperin said dozens of GOP strategists and operatives have shared negative views of the vice president in the embarrassing aftermath of the blue tsunami that saw Democrats wrest control of Congress from Republicans.

news.title: Amid razor-thin Mississippi Senate battle, concerns raised over voter challenges
news.text:
Thousands of affidavit ballots could prove decisive in Mississippi's razor-thin race for U.S. Senate and lawyers representing both Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith are girding for the possiblity of a protracted legal fight over which ballots should be counted. 

The race could be projected as soon as Wednesday. Colom holds a small lead over Hyde-Smith with most of the vote counted.

Affidavit ballots in Mississippi are provisional ballots that allow people to cast a vote even if they show up at the polls without voter ID or do not show up as a registered voter at their polling place.

Officials in Hinds County, which is among the state's largest counties and contains the city of Jackson, finished processing affidavit ballots on Wednesday.

Hinds County is heavily Democratic and voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 by over 40 percentage points. Around 70% of the county's population is Black, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

Questions over many voters' registrations and whether they need to cast affidavit ballots date back to early 2025, when Mississippi officials began deactivating voters from state voter rolls in part by using data from Experian, a credit-reporting company. 

State election leaders said at the time that the Experian data was meant to be used as a supplemental tool by county election officials "to bring a new level of reliable data for county election commissioners to utilize in maintaining Mississippi's voter rolls." 

But an Experian spokesman said its data should not have been used for the purpose of deactivating voters.

"The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records," Scott Anderson, vice president of corporate communications at Experian, told ABC News. "Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws."

An estimated 230,000 voters were deactivated from the state's voter registration lists ahead of the 2026 midterms, according to local news reports and a voting advocacy group. Mississippi Today reported that the Experian data could have led state and local officials to inadvertently deactivate eligible voters from registration lists.

However, a spokesperson for the Mississippi Secretary of State’s office told ABC News on Wednesday that those 230,000 people were not all deemed inactive in 2026 alone, however, as that list “is a cumulative list that is added to as commissioners place people on in active status.”

The spokesperson said it reflects years of work by election commissions in the state, and is not just a reflection of how the Experian data was used.

According to the spokesperson, Experian data pointed to approximately 113,000 individuals for local election officials to review, which included voters identified for review from U.S. Postal Service data and from Experian data.

The office of Mississippi's Secretary of State also told ABC affiliate WAPT that it is not using Experian data anymore and that no voters had their registration deactivated within 90 days before the election, consistent with federal law. 

Colom and voting rights advocates have raised concerns that far more voters are casting affidavit votes because they had their registrations incorrectly deactivated than there should have been, leading to more general challenges for voters.

Colom placed the blame on Secretary of State Michael Watson.

"Experian told him they were not reliable. He did it anyways. So I think that this chaos is the result of that decision, and it's not me just saying it," he said.

Watson, appearing on a talk radio show on Monday, said that the state had found that it couldn't get all of the information from the U.S. Postal Service that it needed about voters who may have moved, but had done a pilot program with Experian in a county and found it helpful. 

Trey Grayson, an attorney and former Kentucky Republican secretary of state, told ABC News that Mississippi did nothing wrong by using Experian data in addition to other data sources and pointed out that voters who had their registrations deactivated incorrectly were still able to cast ballots. 

"I believe that states should use as many valid sources as possible when it comes to list maintenance. Fortunately, the safeguards built into the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) prevent a voter from being purged when a state receives evidence of a move. Instead, those voters are classified as inactive and they are still eligible to vote for the next two federal election cycles so long as they provide evidence of their address."

"This safeguard in the NVRA helps states balance the need to maintain accurate voter rolls with the need to ensure that every eligible voter is able to vote," Grayson wrote.
news.summary: Voting rights advocates say faulty data is causing deactivation of some voters.
news.author: Lucien Bruggeman,Oren Oppenheim

news.title: Explosive new claims about Alex Cooper and Dave Portnoy: Read the dirty details she wants airbrushed from history as feud with ex-Call Her Daddy host Sofia Franklyn goes nuclear
news.text:
The doe-eyed brunette had been scrubbed off the cover. Her high-pitched, valley-girl voice was absent from the show. This would be – as the episode title declared – 'the funeral' of Sofia Franklyn.

'Welcome back to Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper's raspy voice greeted listeners in the first solo episode of the podcast after booting her now-humiliated best friend off the show. 'It is your – now single – father.'

For an hour, Cooper detailed her side of their messy breakup on the May 27, 2020, episode in which she said: 'We're mourning the loss of someone.'

She told fans the 'awful' things that her ex-best friend and former co-host had said in those final days, words she said she could never 'imagine ever saying to a friend.' She complained about having to do all the work, especially as Franklyn repeatedly showed up 'empty-handed.' She thanked the 'Daddy Gang' for siding with her.

As Call Her Daddy was acquired by Dave Portnoy's Barstool Sports then Spotify and finally SiriusXM, Cooper had won – the show, the audience, the tens of millions of dollars tied to Call Her Daddy – all while making Franklyn out as a free-loading villain whose greedy boyfriend led to her spectacularly horrible fall.

And for more than six years, Franklyn, 34, let that narrative prevail. She said she was 'broken' and ill-equipped to take on a public dispute, and knew she 'couldn't compete' with her wildly successful ex-friend. And so, she sat silent while Cooper, 32, became a multi-million-dollar media mogul with her own network and married the love of her life. Her career sidelined, Franklyn could have easily become a digital-age afterthought, but instead, she had been plotting her next move.

After years of seeing Cooper everywhere, Franklyn had decided it's her time now, telling her side of the story in her memoir Daddy Issues, which rehashed every ugly detail in their bitter feud while desperately trying to shed the party girl persona that once made her famous.

It's the hallmark of a reversal of fortunes, because while Cooper's meteoric rise has appeared to have apexed and is now starting its descent thanks to a series of business and relationship fiascos, Franklyn is seizing the moment for her comeback.

On Tuesday, Franklyn published her own account of the internet's messiest breakup, claiming that Cooper had tried to get her fired from the podcast months before their fallout, and alleged how Cooper's jokes on the shows were largely written by someone else.

Franklyn republished some of the emails and texts in her book that she claims corroborate this; Cooper has not publicly commented on it. 

She also speculated that during negotiations, when they were invited to Portnoy's home, Cooper seemingly had been there before.

She wrote: 'His apartment is a mess and looks exactly like the Barstool offices, with the addition of a fish tank. This is the apartment of a short man-child with too much money. I expect Alex to make a joke about the place, but she’s uncharacteristically awkward and doesn’t say a thing. Something gives me the vibe she’s been here before. Jesus Christ, did they f**k or something?'

Cooper has not addressed these claims. Portnoy, however, called the allegations 'fiction' while appearing on The Toast podcast on Wednesday.

When Franklyn announced she would be penning a tell-all, she explained she waited six years to tell her story because she felt she 'needed to grow up and be free of ego as much as humanly possible.'

After all, the ego that comes with immaturity was part of their personas on Call Her Daddy, which became known for raunchy hookup stories and unfiltered, and often inadvisable, sex tips to its millions of listeners worldwide. In arguably their most scandalous episode, they discussed sex techniques 'guaranteed to be every man's kryptonite.'

'It is a vacuum-seal, double-hand twist gluck gluck combo,' Cooper said on the third episode of the show.

'I wish I had a d**k so you could s**k it at this point,' Franklyn laughed.

It's a far cry from Franklyn's Utah upbringing, where she and her younger brother were raised by their immigrant single mother. She attended a private Catholic school that she claimed normalized drugs and sex as a 'counterculture' to the conservative Mormon culture of the state. She wound up moving to New York City and landing a job at Morgan Stanley as a client services associate during her 20s. 

That's when she met Cooper, who was in ad sales for Gotham magazine. In 2018, Franklyn, who had been looking to get out of her apartment, found herself sharing an Uber pool with a stranger who just happened to know a friend who was looking for a roommate.

Franklyn and Cooper hit it off right away. By the end of the day, the pair had signed a lease together.

Franklyn described their fast friendship as 'borderline romantic, in a lot of ways more intimate than a romantic partner.'

'She feels immediately familiar, like someone I've known forever, or even an extension of myself,' she wrote about meeting Cooper for the first time.

Their lives were fully intertwined, living together and partying together. Cooper wondered, why didn't they work together? She suggested they launch a podcast, which they debuted in October 2018. 

Within a month of Call Her Daddy's first episode, their show was bought by Portnoy's Barstool Sports. Franklyn, who was making $55,000 at Morgan Stanley, and Cooper, who was unemployed at the time, each signed a three-year deal that included a $75,000 salary for the first year, with commission on merch sales. 

Their popularity exploded. Call Her Daddy, which introduced X-rated sex terms like 'Cooch Gobbler,' swept college campuses and dominated the group chats of women in their 20s. In two months, episode downloads shot up from just 12,000 to two million downloads, topping podcast charts.

Their show was bringing a whole new audience to the bro-y juggernaut, and yet their compensation remained the same. And with Barstool owning the rights to Call Her Daddy, they couldn't take the show to another network that was willing to cough up more dough.

The co-hosts figured they'd try to strike a deal with Portnoy, but as negotiations dragged on, things became messy. Communication became even more difficult after everyone left the city in the early days of the pandemic, which meant Franklyn and Cooper were no longer living or partying together.

Portnoy eventually agreed to offer them a substantial pay increase – a $500,000 salary each – plus the option to leave with the rights to the show after a year.

Franklyn wanted to walk. Cooper claimed she suspected Franklyn thought there was a bigger deal elsewhere, largely influenced by her then-boyfriend and former HBO executive Peter Nelson, which Franklyn has denied.

'I deserved more than four percent for a show I not only poured my heart and soul into, but exposed every intricate detail about my mental, emotional and sex life on a weekly basis,' Franklyn reflected later in October 2020. 'I know my worth.'

But Cooper was ready to shake Portnoy's hand even if it meant sidelining Franklyn.

'Was she ever my friend?' Franklyn writes in her new memoir. 'She was! I saw it. I felt it. I live in her apartment. Our apartment. I take the train to work with her, and then I sit next to her at work, and then I take the train home with her. Together. And then we go to Bubby's and order pancakes if we feel like it.'

'I think about every contract conversation we've ever had [with Portnoy]. Jokes. How we share every single f**king thing with each other – space, time, emotions, work, pain, highs, shame, heartbreak, family. Alex wouldn't do this,' she wrote of the deal being negotiated behind the scenes.

'Sofia didn't want to take the deal, but I did, so I stayed,' Cooper said in her 2025 Hulu docuseries, Call Her Alex. 'I realized the "Daddy Gang" was bigger than both of us.' 

Cooper privately took the deal with Portnoy after telling Portnoy that Franklyn would be unwilling to do so – a claim Franklyn has denied.

'Alex calls two days later and she says, "Listen, I want to take this deal. Sofia is never going to take this deal,"' Portnoy told Joe Rogan in January 2023.

Franklyn recalled hearing Cooper make a similar claim in a 52-minute-long video called 'The Truth About Call Her Daddy.'

Writing directly to Cooper in her memoir, Franklyn said: 'I told you VERBATIM I would even take the deal to stay. I've done everything to stay together and keep the show alive.'

In every mention of the fallout, Cooper has maintained that Franklyn did not want to do the deal with Portnoy.

When Cooper's one-year contract was up, she took Call Her Daddy – and its catalog of past episodes, IP which Franklyn would not own – to Spotify for a $60 million deal.

Franklyn said she was furious. She was featured in nearly 80 of those shows but would not see 'one penny' from the acquisition. Franklyn and Nelson eventually broke up in 2022 after dating for nearly four years and she later defended her decision to discuss the deal with him, arguing that he was not as involved as the headlines claimed him to be.

'He was my boyfriend. Like, you're obviously going to confide in your boyfriend about your work and everything going on in your life,' she told Jason Tartick's Trading Secrets podcast in June 2025. 

Cooper eventually made even more when she signed with SiriusXM in a multiyear deal reportedly worth $125 million.

On Monday, Franklyn admitted that as friends in their 20s, she and Cooper did not think to sign a partnership agreement before going into business together.

'You don't know how someone is going to behave until the money and the fame show up,' Franklyn told The Bossticks podcast.

The brunette tried to start her own rival show, Sofia with an F, but after peaking at number one upon its debut in 2020, the podcast, which offered a similar unfiltered look at dating and pop culture, flopped.

'With every following week, the episodes lose their newness, I lose my virality and we trend down from number one,' Franklyn reflects in her book.

But aside from the weekly vlog-style episodes that she continues to release every Thursday, Franklyn has had few creative or professional projects until now.

Cooper, on the other hand, with her 'access to millions of people' thanks to the Call Her Daddy brand, became inescapable.

She launched her own podcast network Unwell, a name that longtime listeners have suggested was an original soundbite from Franklyn, signing major talent like influencers Alix Earle and Madeline Argy, as well as actor Owen Thiele and reality TV star Harry Jowsey.

Franklyn was dismayed knowing she would 'have to live the rest of my life haunted by' the catchphrase, which she claims was stolen by her former friend and business partner. Cooper has not addressed who came up with 'unwell,' but fans have pointed to an email that Franklyn discussed on the early days of the podcast in which she called in sick to her job at Morgan Stanley with a note that read 'I'm unwell.'

Talking to podcasters Lauryn and Michael Bosstick, Franklyn contemplated Cooper's decision: 'You have resources, you have a marketing team, why are you using this? Like, have you not taken enough?'

The Pennsylvania-raised blonde fashioned Unwell into a media empire, with the addition of a creative agency and a production company. She also started a beverage company with Nestle, served as an NBC correspondent for the 2024 Paris Olympics and released a two-part Hulu documentary about her life.

Cooper's personal life was also thriving. After years of detailing her sexual escapades with men she nicknamed 'Slim Shady,' 'The Canadian' and 'Red Sox Man,' Cooper was engaged to 'Mr Sexy Zoom Man.' In an intimate celebration in the Riviera Maya, Cooper married film producer Matt Kaplan, the details of their wedding laid bare in a 5,000-word feature in Vogue Weddings. 

Franklyn, still silent at the time, was envious.

'It becomes impossibly clear to me how much Alex has eclipsed me: the riches, the Forbes cover, the refined beauty, the celebrity guests, the SKIMS campaign that keeps popping up when I'm mid-bedtime routine, the Miu Miu flats. The husband, the Pinterest-perfect wedding covered by Vogue, the breeded dogs,' Franklyn wrote.

'I know I can't compete with her anymore.'

As Cooper made the rounds in media for her business ventures, so too did Franklyn when she married London-based financier John Messamore in a lavish, three-day lakeside summer wedding in Lake Como, a celebration that was exclusively covered by the Times.

And if Cooper somehow missed the wedding announcement, Franklyn is embarking on a five-city book tour, starting in New York, where tickets are already sold out and finishing in her hometown of Salt Lake City.

And in what could be a subtle dig to Cooper, Franklyn will along the way head to Los Angeles, where Cooper now lives with her husband and newborn son, and Boston, famously Cooper's college town, which they used to share stories together of their exploits.

Cooper, on the other hand, has had a rocky year.

Earlier this year, a series of damning reports published by Bloomberg and Vanity Fair alleged in April that Cooper and her husband had cultivated a 'toxic' workplace at Unwell, resulting in a high turnover rate not only among lower-level staff but also among high-level executives.

At least 30 current and former employees told Vanity Fair that Kaplan, who largely runs the day-to-day operations at Unwell, repeatedly made young female employees cry as he berated them over mistakes and threatened to withhold payment.

There were also allegations that Kaplan made uncomfortable remarks to female staff, asking personal questions about their sex lives and commenting frequently on their physical appearance.

Shortly after the story broke, Cooper refuted those claims, suggesting to the Wall Street Journal that those accusations were part of a 'smear campaign' against her and her husband.

'I will just kind of leave it at, "Don't believe everything that you read on the internet,"' she said in June.

Kaplan has never publicly commented on those accusations. 

A couple of months later, sources at Target, Unwell Beverages' main retail and distribution partner, told Bloomberg that Cooper's drink line was shutting down less than two years after hitting the shelves. Then a few weeks later, the podcaster's dating show, Love Overboard, was canceled after just one season on air.

She's also lost some fans since going from sex smoke show to Gen Z's Barbara Walters. For her solo act, Cooper has traded her personal explicit stories for more serious interviews with high-profile guests like former Vice President Kamala Harris, former First Lady Michelle Obama, Monica Lewinsky, Hailey Bieber and Jane Fonda. But rather than mature with her target audience, some fans think the 32-year-old's show has become 'bland' and lost its ability to offer 'anything new or revolutionary.'

'I stopped listening because I miss what call her daddy was,' one Reddit user said. 'I'm now 30 so of course we grow up and change but I didn't sign up to listen to celebs everyday my God.'

All of this arrived on the heels of yet another Cooper spat that ricocheted across the internet. A year and a half after signing TikTok megastar Earle to her Unwell network in 2023, Cooper became embroiled in a vitriolic fallout with her protege.

At one point, the older blonde publicly called Earle out in a TikTok, baiting the 25-year-old to 'get specific and just say what you gotta say about me.'

But Earle waited until the premiere of her own Netflix docuseries Earle Meets World to divulge any details. In a scene where she addresses Cooper's confrontational video, she told her family she had been 'taken advantage of and used and mistreated and manipulated' by her 'idol.'

Breaking down into tears, the influencer recounted how Cooper asked her 'really sexual questions' on camera while she was drunk, leading her to answer in ways she could 'never take back.'

Cooper has not responded to Earle's claims.

Franklyn's fans, vocal on Reddit, felt vindicated by Earle's claim. They believed they had seen this movie before.

In her memoir, Franklyn reveals that ahead of the book's publication, her book agent called, informing her that Cooper and Kaplan were threatening to sue. Neither Cooper nor Kaplan have commented on this publicly.

'It's the first I've heard from Alex in six years,' Franklyn wrote. 'The first time since the fallout, when she stopped responding to my text messages. Only it isn't her talking. It's her husband, Matt, talking for her. A man I've never met.'

Franklyn previously told fans in an October 30 vlog that she heard that Cooper's husband has been 'trying to get his hands' on her memoir, reaching out to publicists and Franklyn's acquaintances.

'They play gross and dirty,' she said of her ex-best friend and Kaplan.

Neither Cooper nor Kaplan have responded to Franklyn's remarks. 

The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Franklyn, Cooper, Kaplan and Portnoy for comment.

For a moment, it appeared that Cooper could escape the scrutiny.

In a TikTok video responding to Cooper and Kaplan's May pregnancy announcement, Portnoy said the podcaster had played 'a trump card.'

'Once you're pregnant, all the haters gotta zip it,' the Barstool founder said of Cooper, who welcomed a baby boy on October 20.

The timing, for Franklyn's return, couldn't be any better.
news.summary: After years of seeing Alex Cooper everywhere, Sofia Franklyn had decided it's her time to tell her side of the story.

news.title: Scott Colom Makes History With Mississippi Senate Win, CNN Projects
news.text: Scott Colom is projected to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John C. Stennis in 1982, CNN projected Wednesday, in a historic victory that would also make him the first Black Mississippian popularly elected to the chamber. Colom, a local prosecutor, unseated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. The victory came more than a week after midterm elections that saw Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress. As of Wednesday night, 98.6 percent of ballots had been tallied, with Colom leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent. Despite CNN's projection, the Associated Press has not yet called the race. Cindy Hyde-Smith vs. Scott Colom: What Final Polls Showed Hyde-Smith led in polls in the run up to Election Day. A Change Research survey of 842 voters conducted October 21 to 22 placed Hyde-Smith at 43 percent support and Colom at 40 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. A Data for Progress poll conducted August 5 to 15 had Hyde-Smith on 44 percent and Colom on 38 percent. It surveyed 1,018 likely voters and had a 3-point margin of error. Why Mississippi Senate Race Is Critical to Midterms Mississippi’s result means the balance of power in Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s second term slides further in the Democrats' favor. The president’s party has historically tended to lose congressional seats in midterm elections. Trump won the state by nearly 23 percentage points in 2024, receiving 60.9 percent of the vote to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 38 percent. This election featured races for 35 Senate seats. Democrats held 13 of the seats up for grabs, compared with 22 held by Republicans. Republicans went into Election Day with a 53-47 majority in the Senate. The Democratic Party sought to win back Congress while the Republicans hoped to hold on to their majorities in both chambers. Democrats took control of the House Tuesday, flipping key seats in Texas, Iowa, Nebraska, Wisconsin, North Carolina, Kentucky, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Colorado. The GOP also lost the Senate, with Democrats wresting control of seats in Texas, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, Maine and South Carolina. For more analysis on the numbers shaping U.S. politics and the 2026 midterms, sign up for Newsweek's Midterms Monitor newsletter. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: Colom became Mississippi's first Democratic Senate winner since 1982 and its first Black popularly elected senator.

news.title: Democrats are most excited to support three candidates for 2028
news.text: If the 2026 midterms were an opportunity for voters to express their feelings about President Donald Trump’s administration, the election in two years will be their first opportunity to cast a vote for president without his name on the ballot.Trump is constitutionally barred from running again, which means, as the lame duck portion of his presidency comes into view, it’s not too early to start thinking about who might replace him.Potential candidates certainly are. While they might bat away speculation, many are starting to think seriously about their potential path or wrestling with the ultimate question — is it worth the investment of time and energy and the guarantee of being vilified by your political rivals in the off chance that you could be the most powerful person in the world?RELATED STORY | Kamala Harris returns to campaign trail as 2028 speculation growsA little more than half of Americans, 54%, have given at least some thought to the coming presidential race, according to a CNN Poll conducted by SSRS in the month before the midterm election. Fewer, 40%, said they’re looking forward to it, with 27% saying they’re dreading it and the rest expressing neither outlook.No major candidate has yet declared a campaign, although the first of those could come sooner than many people think.Most Americans don’t yet have a 2028 candidate in mindAbout a third of Americans, 35%, said there’s a specific candidate they’d like to see run, compared to 64% who are taking more of a wait-and-see attitude.The two Republican politicians whose names were most frequently mentioned were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, at 8%, and Vice President JD Vance at 7%. President Donald Trump has joked about the two men being rivals or even forming a ticket together. Rubio has said he would defer to Vance.Among Democratic politicians, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (3%), former Vice President and Democrats’ 2024 nominee Kamala Harris (2%), and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (2%) were the only potential candidates to get the attention of more than 1% of Americans in the poll.Things changed when Americans were asked by pollsters about specific candidates.Harris is the most known DemocratAbout a quarter of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would be excited to support Harris (27%), Rep, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (27%), and Buttigieg (26%). Slightly fewer (22%) said they would be excited to support Newsom or Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona and 16% expressed excitement about Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia.The poll was conducted before the midterms, however, and Ossoff has clearly generated some buzz. He won the straw poll at a conference for Democratic activists, Crooked Con, held the weekend after Ossoff’s commanding reelection in Georgia. He has said he has no interest in running for president.Harris has the most total support. More than three-quarters of Democrats and Democratic leaners (51%) said that they would at least consider backing her. But she is also the most well-known of the candidates. Just 7% said they didn’t know enough about her to offer an opinion, compared with 55% who said the same of Ossoff. Harris also had the highest portion of Democratic-aligned adults, 15%, who said they would never support her.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meetingMore than 60% said they didn’t know enough about some other potential candidates, including Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, all of whom have been mentioned as potential candidates.Midterms could also have buoyed someone like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who handily won reelection and also helped flip multiple house seats to Democrats in his swing state. In CNN’s poll, just 10% said they’d be excited to support him, 28% said they’d consider it, and 54% said they didn’t have enough information.Vance and Rubio generate excitementVance and Rubio get similar marks from Republicans and Republican leaners: 41% said they would be excited to support Vance and 41% said they would be excited to support Rubio. news.title: Mississippi elects Democratic senator in major upset for GOP: CNN
news.text:
The last Democrat to represent Mississipi in the United States Senate, John Stennis, was a staunch segregationist. Now, more than three decades after Stennis left office, an African American district attorney named Scott Colom has become the first Democrat to serve Mississippi in the Senate since the Cold War, CNN reports.

Running against incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-MS), Colom is a northern Mississippi district attorney who was obscure outside his home state prior to being thrust into the national limelight. Mississippi is an overwhelmingly Republican state where Hyde-Smith served a single term as senator and wished to serve a second one. Raised in a privileged family and attending a segregated private school in Mississippi, Hyde-Smith was a career politician who developed a rivalry with Colom after she blocked the Democrat's nomination to a federal judgeship.

Prior to Colom's surprisingly strong showing, few observers regarded Mississippi as being a potential pick-up state for the United States Senate. Even as President Donald Trump's approval rating plummeted and Republicans became vulnerable in ostensibly conservative states like Iowa, South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, Hyde-Smith was regarded as safe in a state that Trump won by 61 percent to 38 percent for the Democratic nominee, Vice President Kamala Harris. Like Harris, Colom is a person color running against someone waging an explicitly racial campaign in a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since Gov. Ronnie Musgrove's sole term ended in 2004.

As the results for Colom came in last Wednesday, MS NOW's longtime election analyst Steve Kornacki marveled at the highly unexpected nature of Colom's win.

"Listen, there's like, Lowndes County, 1,200 votes left. Colom is winning that by about 16 points, so he'll net votes from there," Kornacki told MS NOW viewers. "Jackson County, we've got about 1,600 votes. Hyde-Smith — they probably cancel each other out. I'm seeing a lot of counties that will probably cancel each other out. And the big thing that's jumping out at this is that the most remaining vote is in Hinds County. And of all the counties where there's remaining vote, where there's significant remaining vote, it's the one where a candidate has the most lopsided advantage. You know, Colom leading that by 60 points."

He later concluded, in astonishment, "You're looking at, really, a possibility here of Colom, the Democrat, winning this race."

Hyde-Smith's team also struggled to accept that Colom could win, especially as the margin between the two candidates narrowed to two digits.

"With the vast majority of Election Day ballots reported, the margin is measured in just dozens of votes," Hyde-Smith's team wrote during the counting process. "We have thousands of outstanding ballots, including affidavit and absentee ballots, which still must be processed and verified under Mississippi law."

Hyde-Smith added, "Our campaign is closely monitoring the remaining count. We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith."

news.title: Group backing AOC for 2028 White House run recruits 10,000 supporters in 24 hours
news.text:
A grassroots group backing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for president in 2028 says it signed up thousands of supporters in its first 24 hours. 

“Ready for AOC” recruited “over 10,000 supporters from across all 50 states” in its first 24 hours, a spokesperson told The Independent Wednesday. The group is not affiliated with the congresswoman’s campaign.

“AOC is the only candidate who can lead the working class movement to fight the oligarchy and transform America,” the group wrote in its inaugural social media post Monday. “We’re organizing across the country to build the grassroots support we need to win in 2028.”

About 4,000 of those supporters have committed to attending welcome calls over the next month. “People are clearly ready to be a part of something transformational,” a group spokesperson also told Politico. “They’re ready to put in the work.”

The recruitment push comes after Democrats romped to victory in a string of red states, reclaiming control of the House and the Senate in last week’s midterm elections.

Ocasio-Cortez, a 37-year-old New York progressive Democrat, has long been seen as a potential White House contender, with polls placing her near the top of the prospective Democratic field.

An outspoken Trump critic, she frequently uses social media to explain her policies and talk candidly to her millions of followers. She has also traveled the country with Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont Independent, on their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.

Ocasio-Cortez, who was first elected to Congress in 2018, has also left the door open to a presidential bid. Asked about running in August, she said: “I haven’t ruled out the possibility. And I’m very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there.” 

When questioned about a theoretical match-up against Vice President JD Vance last year, she said she would “stomp him.”

Other Democrats floated as potential 2028 contenders include California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

One Democrat whose national profile has risen sharply is Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, who won re-election last week with 59 percent of the vote.

Over the past month, Ossoff’s odds of winning the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination have surged in online prediction platforms. He now leads the field on both Kalshi and Polymarket, putting him at least 10 percentage points ahead of Ocasio-Cortez on each platform.

Ossoff would be “a slam dunk number one pick,” polling analyst Nate Silver said last week. “He seems like the uniformly ‘compromise candidate’ between the progressive and the more centrist factions of the party. And he seems very talented.”
news.summary: ‘AOC is the only candidate who can lead the working class movement to fight the oligarchy and transform America,’ the grassroots group said

news.title: Financially-Squeezed Voters Made Jaw-Dropping 60-Point Swing Toward Democrats Since 2024
news.text:
Voters who said they were financially struggling made a 60-point swing toward Democrats between the 2024 presidential election and the midterms, a NORC/Washington Post survey found. 

Sixty-four percent of voters who said they were economically “falling behind” voted for Democratic House candidates, while 33% voted for Republicans, according to a NORC/Washington Post survey. This bloc of voters supported Trump over former Vice President Kamala Harris by over 30 points in 2024, showing a dramatic shift in partisan support. 

Twenty-nine percent of the 90,000 voters surveyed said they were struggling financially, 58% said they were “holding steady” and 12% said they were getting ahead, according to the survey. Of those holding steady, 52% supported Democrats and 45% supported Republicans. Fifty-nine percent of those getting ahead voted for Republicans. 

One in five independent voters supported Democrats by more than 20 points, a much larger margin than those who supported Harris over Trump, according to the poll. Nearly seven in ten independents supported Democratic Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, while about two-thirds of independents supported Democratic Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. (RELATED: Exit Pollsters Didn’t Bother Asking Jewish Voters About Iran War Views)

In case you had any questions about some of what went down on Tuesday night… https://t.co/mYScNSmPP0— Ned Ryun (@nedryun) November 10, 2026

Trump made historic inroads with Latino voters and with young men who were unsatisfied with the economy in 2024. Voters within those demographics who were most concerned with the economy voted for Democrats in 2026. 

Forty-five percent of Hispanics believed the economy was the most important issue facing the U.S., while 15% said immigration, according to the exit poll. Sixty-two percent of Hispanic voters said the cost of living was “crucial” to their vote, according to the exit poll. The vast majority, 70% and 57%, of those respondents voted for Democrats.

Prices of energy, gas, food and other goods surged since the start of Iran war. The average price of gas cost $3.94 per gallon as of Wednesday, up from $3.07 per gallon from the year prior, according to AAA. Diesel prices rose from $3.74 per gallon in November 2025 to $6.13 per gallon.

Voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war, prompting them to vote for Democrats. Forty-four percent of respondents said their financial situation was worse than two years ago and 18% said they were better off, according to an NBC News poll from Nov. 3. 

Young men voted for Democrats by a 17-point margin after backing Trump in 2024. A survey by Harvard Youth Poll found that 27% of young people believed they were financially worse off than their parents, while 25% believed they were better off. 

Generation Z showed the lowest levels of support for the Iran war among all generations surveyed by Navigator Research. Only 30% of Gen Z supported the war, while 44% of Baby Boomers and 55% of the Silent Generation supported Trump’s military actions.
news.summary: Financially struggling voters abandoned their support for Trump

news.title: Now That Democrats Won The Midterms, Is ‘Woke’ Coming Back?
news.text:
As the midterm results rolled in last Tuesday, there was one common refrain I kept seeing: woke is back, baby! We’re inventing five new genders, every Thanksgiving prayer gotta start with a land acknowledgment, and we’re remaking every John Wayne movie with a queer, nonbinary lead actor. That’s just the law now, folks. Deal with it.

In all seriousness, though, the overwhelming victory by Democrats during last week’s midterms left me wondering if ‘woke’ is making a comeback. Woke has been co-opted by the right as a disparaging term to label anything that doesn’t center straight, white men with so-called Christian values, but personally, I wear woke as a badge of honor, cause f-k those cornballs. 

With that said, the 2024 election just felt awful, y’all. Now, I never really believed that Trump’s election win was an absolute rejection of diversity and progressive values. The economy was (and still is) in rough shape, and Kamala Harris was given very little time to introduce herself to voters and establish a succinct campaign message. People felt the economy was getting worse; the Democrats didn’t do a great job of explaining why the economy was getting worse, and Trump coasted to victory by making false promises of lowering prices and not starting any new wars. 

Despite Trump winning by normal margins amid depressed voter turnout, major corporations wasted no time backpedaling on their commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. Target was one of the biggest, uh, targets, as it announced an end to its DEI initiatives before Trump passed any legislation banning the practice. Movie studios wasted no time removing LGBTQ elements from their movies and burying their shows with Black leads.

Things were bad, but thanks to last week’s election results, we can safely say reports on the death of woke have been greatly exaggerated. 

State legislators in Texas are already working to reinstate diversity, equity, and inclusion programs at publicly funded colleges and universities. In my home state of Arizona, voters struck down an anti-DEI prop with 60% of the vote. Mind you, Arizona has historically been the definition of a purple state.

Chris Pappas made history by becoming the first openly gay Senator after winning his race in New Hampshire. In fact, we saw a litany of firsts on election night! From Keisha Lance Bottoms becoming the first Black woman to ever become governor, Abdul Al-Sayed becoming the first Muslim senator, to Gina Hinojosa flipping the Texas governor’s seat and becoming the state’s first Latina governor in the process. 

The idea that Americans are against diversity and progressive values was decisively rejected by absurdly high margins last week. Add to that the fact that companies that maintained their DEI initiatives faced no financial repercussions and were viewed more favorably by consumers, and I wouldn’t be surprised if we see corporations bending over backward to show their progressive values.

In fact, the absolute piledriver that Democrats gave Republicans last week had me very curious about the direction Skydance is going to take with the content it produces. Skydance Co-CEO David Ellison and his father, Larry Ellison, have gotten quite close to the Trump administration. David threw several dinners for Trump ahead of the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, and even attended this year’s State of the Union with late Sen. Lindsay Graham. 

So clearly, David Ellison has sympathies for the Republican Party, which made it all the more surprising when he said that James Gunn and Peter Safran would continue to run DC Studios after the merger, given their slate of DC films were Peak Woke™. Turns out that was a lie, as Ellison fired Gunn and Safran earlier this week. 

Who did Ellison replace them with? A conservative Christian who considers whether or not a movie will play to his grandma in his decision-making. The official reasoning given by Skydance was that Superman and Lanterns didn’t hit the numbers they wanted and had no cultural impact. As a result, the DCU is changing direction, and Lanterns is not getting renewed for a season two.

To say that Superman and Lanterns had no cultural impact makes me incredibly curious what culture David Ellison is paying attention to. Because the actual audience really isn’t that opposed to “wokeness,” despite what incels and bots on Twitter would lead you to believe. 

It’s why Sinners was a sensation last year, why Lanterns was all anyone was talking about every Sunday, and why One Battle After Another crushed it at the Oscars last year. It’s why Heated Rivalry, an explicitly queer love story, is one of the biggest shows of the year. Black stories, queer stories, and politically complicated stories are still driving the culture, despite what corporations try to tell us. 

With Skydance, we’re seeing a company double down on a viewpoint Americans have rejected with both their vote and their dollar. I’m curious to see if Hollywood at large is going to continue its walkback on diversity, or if they’re going to reverse course and lean into the Blue wave. 

The question “Is woke coming back?” was rhetorical, because if pop culture and the recent election have shown us anything, it’s that people didn’t lose their appetite for progressive values.

Democrats Won Big In The Midterms, But They Still Dropped The Ball
news.summary: With Democrats controlling 75% of states and controlling Congress by decisive margins, can we stop acting like the streets aren’t yearning for “woke”?

news.title: Mark Halperin’s 2028 Democratic Power Rankings Have One Big Problem
news.text:
Veteran political journalist Mark Halperin has released his first “8 for ’28” rankings of potential Democratic presidential contenders since the midterm elections, but as with any early horse race, he acknowledges there’s a chance many of those on the list won’t even run for president. Also, the two men at the top share one enormous problem.

Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-Pa.) and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) claim the top two spots, in that order, after convincingly winning reelection in battleground states.

The two men were the biggest winners of the midterms, and Halperin argues they are the only two Democrats most Republicans he talks to genuinely fear facing in a general election. Ossoff jumped from No. 8 on last month’s list, and Halperin says he easily could have ranked him No. 1 after talking with Democratic sources, who were most impressed by both men’s communication and fundraising abilities.

But the obvious problem is that both are Jewish, a big negative for the increasingly antisemitic Democratic Party. Halperin wonders whether two hypothetical developments might make that more palatable: Benjamin Netanyahu no longer being Israel’s prime minister and the Iran war receding from the headlines. He also notes that Ossoff is less culturally Jewish and observant than Shapiro, so “maybe he cheats the difference there.”

If you think the antisemites in the Democratic Party will be okay with a Jew who doesn’t observe the Sabbath and criticizes Netanyahu, watch this video of California state Sen. Scott Wiener (D-11th District), who is Jewish and as progressive as they come, being harassed at a trans march in San Francisco.

Nevertheless, Halperin says Republicans like National Review Editor-in-Chief Rich Lowry fear Ossoff right now because of one thing: electability. Halperin points to not only his Obama-esque cadences but also the similarity of his campaign logos to Barack Obama’s, a sign that he’s going after that hope-and-change vibe. PJ Media Managing Editor Chris Queen, who lives in Georgia, wrote about how Ossoff seems to think he’s the next Obama in a piece earlier this year. 

Maybe in select clips, he can pull that off, but Chris’s analysis from on the ground in Georgia suggests he’d have a lot of trouble duplicating Obama’s electoral success were he ever to get the nomination: "Ossoff is undoubtedly an ambitious little dweeb, and he obviously has enough Obama-level arrogance to think that he’s presidential material. Ask any normal Georgia resident, and he or she will tell you otherwise."

When Ossoff Claims His Support for Israel Is 'Ironclad,' I Wonder If He Knows What the Word Means

While the prediction markets currently have Ossoff at No. 1, Halperin went with Shapiro in the top spot because he still thinks the governor is more likely to run than the senator, whose kids are only 4 and 1, although he acknowledges that Ossoff may be the best guy to unite the socialist and establishment wings of the party.

But the socialists will still have a candidate, and Halperin says New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-14th District) is the most likely, which is why he has her at No. 3 on the list. Others could join her in the top 8 in future rankings: there’s a group trying to get California Rep. Ro Khanna (D-17th District) to run, and he doesn’t rule out Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) taking one more crack at it.

While Halperin doesn’t have AOC on the list of those whom Republicans most fear facing in a general election, one Republican, former Daily Wire CEO Jeremy Boreing, thinks they should fear her. In this clip, he calls her a generational political talent and warns his party not to underestimate her instincts.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) held the top spot in most of Halperin’s previous rankings but fell to No. 4 this month because Halperin thinks AOC, Ossoff, and Shapiro have more momentum after the midterms. “If you told me Shapiro, Ossoff, AOC, and Newsom weren’t running, I wouldn’t be the least bit surprised,” Halperin said.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, whom Halperin ranks fifth, is the only one in the top five who Halperin is sure is entering the race. He’s also unsure whether Kamala Harris (No. 6) and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), at No. 8, will launch a bid. In Halperin’s view, Gov. Andy Beshear (No. 7) is the one other safe bet to seek the nomination.

According to Halperin, the “Democratic nomination is extremely valuable” right now in the wake of the party’s midterm success because the eventual nominee will likely be favored to win. Ben Shapiro seems to agree. On November 5, he said, “Whatever happens among the Republican candidates, 2028 is obviously an uphill battle for Republicans now.”

An uphill battle, perhaps, but looking at the names on Halperin’s list, it’s one Republicans should welcome.

news.title: Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
news.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent. 

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory. 

“I’ll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media. 

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011. 

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. 

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction. 

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states. 

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker. 

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October. 

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices. 

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

news.text:
Ooh, this is exciting: a totally new, never-before-imagined political theory that explains why the Republicans lost the midterms, how we can rebound, why President Donald Trump has been so successful — and how he can be again. 

Because the party that masters this theory will dominate American politics in 2028, 2032, and beyond.

Feel free to dissect, discuss, debate, and debunk. (This must be what Elon Musk felt like when he invited that guy to hurl a steel ball at a Cybertruck’s windows.) Seriously, I look forward to your feedback.

Okay, no more stalling. Here’s the theory — and our new guiding PR principle: “Today’s political wars are won on the wings of confirmation bias.”

And they’re lost by it, too.

It’s a sign of the times, because the medium makes the message, and today, the monoculture is dead. There is no “arena of ideas” because there are no ideological arenas: Ideas are supposed to battle in a public square, but public squares no longer exist.

Instead of public squares, we now have echo chambers. Dozens and dozens of echo chambers.

Liberals have ‘em, conservatives have ‘em, Zoomers have ‘em, and Boomers have ‘em. Unfortunately, these echo chambers get increasingly sycophantic, closed-off, and “echo-y” because everything runs on an algorithm, and these algorithms prioritize engagement patterns. 

Over time, these patterns deepen. Eventually, they calcify.

This further amplifies our biases.

For most of American history, elections were won by winning hearts and minds. It was literally why we had public debates! Winning hearts and minds was the strategy behind Thomas Paine’s pamphlets during the American Revolution, FDR’s fireside chats, and the use of emotional, gut-wrenching imagery during the Civil Rights movement.

From pamphlets to radio to television, American patriots brilliantly leveraged the most dominant form of mass communication of their era. Each time, the medium shaped the message, and the message won hearts and minds. They competed in the “arena of ideas” and emerged victorious.

But they did so in a public square, and public squares don’t exist anymore.

We can still reach people in echo chambers. (Spend enough money on advertising and PR, and you can reach pretty much anyone.) That’s not the problem.

The problem is that we won’t win their hearts and minds.

Invading an opponent’s echo chamber and convincing him to change his opinion is next to impossible. Too much of a home-field advantage. We can elevate awareness, but echo chambers reverberate with institutional noise, themes, norms, rules, and momentum. Visitors are outnumbered, marginalized, and drowned out. Persuasion is extraordinarily unlikely.

This means a strategy built on winning hearts and minds is a waste of money.

The Republican Party spent BILLIONS on that strategy in the midterms. We blanketed the airwaves with thousands of ads!

Republican groups lost $1.1 billion in midterm Senate races while Democrat groups only lost $12 million, despite spending just over half of that of Republicans, at $677 million. Learn what someone already believes — his biases, assumptions, and philosophical north stars — and tailor your message accordingly. It’s how we exploit echo chambers. It’s how we navigate a world without a monoculture, public squares, or arenas with dueling ideas.

We’re not arguing with the audience anymore — we’re agreeing with them.

Most of PR is designed around confirmation bias: We figure out what the public already likes, and then we try to connect those qualities to a person, brand, or product. It’s also why endorsement deals and spokesmen are so valuable: A celebrity endorsement is a “cheat code” that transfers the positive attributes of the celeb onto whatever you’re selling.

Confirmation bias is human nature. We search, interpret, favor, and recall information that reinforces our beliefs. 

And, of course, we do the opposite with the information that doesn’t.

We see it all the time in politics: Confirmation bias produces the biggest blind spots! It’s amazing!

This is something the GOP would be wise to attack.
