Because Trump was “too dangerous” — and “democracy dies in darkness.”

In 2024, the messaging that validated the audience’s confirmation bias won; the messaging that ran counter to it lost. It fueled Donald Trump’s landslide victory.

The Democrats argued that affordability is still a major problem, Trump policies (i.e., trade wars, the Iran War, and tariffs) made the problem worse, and the president is focusing on vanity projects, ballrooms, and increasing his own net worth instead of helping normal Americans. Lean into the audience’s beliefs. Tailor your messaging for each echo chamber. Blindside the enemy by using his confirmation bias as camouflage. news.title: It’s impeachment season! After the attempt on Pete Hegseth, will Donald Trump be next? | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
The days are getting shorter, the nights are getting longer and some Republicans are getting nervous. After a long stretch of impunity, it’s impeachment season in the US. While the attempt to impeach the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, failed yesterday, Donald Trump may be worried he’s next.

In January, the president warned Republicans that they had better win the November elections or he would be in big trouble. “If we don’t win the midterms … they’ll find a reason to impeach me,” Trump said. He repeated this plea to voters during an October rally in Oklahoma: “Pretend I’m running, please. Just pretend. ’Cause I am on the ballot. And if we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”

I don’t need to tell you what happened with the midterms, do I? The Republicans didn’t just lose – they were given a thrashing so thorough that, for a while, Trump seemed to avoid talking about it. Indeed, in his first public appearance after the election, Trump largely avoided the issue for a full 20 minutes while talking about his beloved White House ballroom project, rhapsodising about its “magnificent” columns. This week, Trump seems to have moved on to another obsession: he is now making baseless claims that the election was rigged. Still, while Trump may be in la-la land half the time, in his moments of lucidity you have to imagine he’s worried a comeuppance is coming.

There are various ways Trump could be held accountable for any alleged crimes, but what he seems most worried about right now is potential impeachment. It’s a multistep process used to charge a public official with serious misconduct and remove them from office. First, articles of impeachment are brought, then the House votes on whether to adopt these articles via a majority vote. If that happens, the person is impeached. But this is where things get tricky. For the official to get removed, the Senate has to hold an impeachment trial and two-thirds of members (67 senators) have to find them guilty; a tough hurdle to clear. There have only been eight cases where this has happened and all the officials removed have been judges.

Trump has already made history by being the only president to have been impeached twice: in 2019 and 2021. In both cases the Senate acquitted him. But now that Democrats have control of government, could Trump become the first president to be removed from office through impeachment?

The short answer is that, while it’s not impossible, it’s unlikely. The Democrats have a majority, but they still only have 54 seats. Attempting to remove Trump would be a gruelling process that many don’t have the appetite for. Kamala Harris said recently: “Going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea … we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations.”

In an interview with NBC News on Sunday, Senator Bernie Sanders went even further. “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Sanders said. “We have to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”

Hear me out: how about we do both? And look, if impeachment is unrealistic, we can get a little creative and come up with other ways to give Trump and his lackeys a small taste of the misery they have inflicted on the rest of us. I would suggest exiling the president to an island and forcing him to listen to his incoherent speeches on a nonstop loop, but I suspect he’d quite enjoy that. Although we could fill the place with wind turbines, which enrage him, and make sure the water is filled with sharks. Trump is weirdly obsessed with the fish; according to Stormy Daniels he once said: “I hope all the sharks die.”

Oh dear, I think I’d better stop there before I have the FBI knocking on my door. Forget the sharks, OK? If the legal system fails us, let’s just focus on replacing him at the next election.

 Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

news.title: Joe Biden says he wouldn’t have run for second term in 2024 if he knew he had cancer
news.text:
Joe Biden said he was unaware of his cancer diagnosis during his presidency and would not have pursued a second term had he known about the illness.

The former Democratic president's remarks came during an interview with People magazine ahead of the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.

"If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer," said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, "I would’ve not gone forward" with his 2024 reelection bid, which ended following a poor debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.

Biden received a diagnosis of metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.

"I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running" for president, Biden remarked in the interview.

However, he maintained that the June 2024 debate, taking place under five months before Election Day, was not a defining event, even as it intensified concerns among Democrats regarding his age — 81 at the time — and his capacity to defeat Trump.

"First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t," Biden said. "But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential."

Within weeks of the debate, Biden withdrew from the race and endorsed his vice president, Kamala Harris, who captured the nomination but ultimately lost to Trump in the general election.

Biden insisted he remained fully capable of serving while in office, arguing that age brought essential experience and deep relationships with international leaders rather than serving as a disqualification.

"I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job," he said.

In August, his son Hunter told the BBC that the cancer had spread, causing his father significant suffering. "It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects," he said.

Since Joe Biden left office, his son has taken on a more prominent public persona, debating Republicans on social media platforms, publishing long commentary on national affairs, and launching a cryptocurrency.

Joe Biden defended his son's public role and his decision to grant Hunter Biden a pardon after the younger Biden's 2024 federal gun conviction and tax charge guilty plea. Hunter Biden had previously endured years of intense Republican scrutiny over his foreign business affairs.

While Hunter Biden noted that the pardon compromised his father's legacy, the former president maintained that Trump's vengeful nature made the action necessary.

"He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do," Joe Biden said. "If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me — he would go back and try to do harm to them."

Biden described his son as "one of the brightest men I know," adding, "I’m really proud of him."
news.summary: Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025

news.title: Democrats May Have Won Big In The Midterms, But In Some Ways, They Still Dropped The Ball
news.text:
So, we all know that Republicans suffered a massive blowout during the midterm elections this month. It has been a sad time for the MAGA world, and a wonderful time for everyone who wanted to see that movement defeated. While polls consistently predicted a blue wave, they underestimated how thoroughly the other side would lose. Roughly 94% of counties across the U.S. shifted blue compared to the 2024 elections. Jurisdictions in all 50 states reported an average 13-point shift toward Democratic House candidates, and not a single one showed an overall shift toward Republicans in the House. Republicans also lost seven seats to Democrats in the U.S. Senate.

Yes, it was bad for Team Red. Horrible, actually.

But what if I told you it could have been worse? What if I told you Democrats may have flipped even more races if not for establishment Democrats who are far too married to the idea that progressives are too far left to be electable, and moderates are still the ones who control the party?

And, look, according to CNN, moderate Democrats did fare better than their progressive counterparts this election cycle — but did it have to be that way?

Take, for example, Angie Nixon in Florida, a state that remained a red spot in the bluetopia that the U.S. became on Nov. 3. In the state that could arguably be viewed as the Black history-hating capital of the nation, Nixon only lost her U.S. Senate race to GOP incumbent Rep. Ashley Moody. According to Axios, Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in Florida since 2012, and Republicans outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million registered voters. Yet, Nixon only lost by about two points.

In a midterm race where Democrats were dominating their Republican opponents by double digits in some races, such as Senator-elect James Talarico, who decimated Republican Ken Paxton to become the first Democratic Senator to be elected in Texas since the late 1980s, Nixon, who was considered one of the longest of longshots to win, was only narrowly defeated.

Imagine what she might have done if the Democrats who controlled the money funded her properly.

Back in September, Nixon told MS NOW that she made a phone call to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, hoping for help funding her race, a request that every candidate poses to their party’s leader. She said his answer was noncommittal.

“When I did speak with Sen. Schumer on the phone, it was basically a ‘we will see,’” Nixon said. He’s going to look into it. That’s what was said, that he’s going to look into it.”

Now, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee told the network at the time that it was ” excited about opportunities to expand the map further and monitor all races closely, including Florida, where Angie Nixon is running an energetic campaign.”

OK, but where was the committee’s energy? Did it match Nixon’s?

According to her, nah.

From MS NOW:

Nixon, a state representative from Jacksonville, won Florida’s Democratic Senate nomination last month in an upset. Her account offers a rare look at how national Democrats are handling a nominee who started as an insurgent, running against the same party establishment that now controls the purse strings.

Nixon and Schumer have yet to have an official meeting in person, though they saw each other last week at an event and spoke. “We are working on a sit-down,” Nixon told MS NOW. “I have talked to some of his staff.”

Asked whether the national party was doing enough to help her win, she was measured but direct: “They could do a lot more.”

Nixon has two explanations for why she believes party leaders are holding back. The first is ideological.

“I am a progressive Democrat, and I am very vocal about putting working-class families first. I am very vocal about progressive values,” she said. “So I think that may be the main issue.”

The second is her race and gender. “Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman, and so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South.”

So, here’s what gets lost in all these conversations about whether Democrats should start leaning toward what people call the “far left,” or whether they should promote more moderate candidates so as not to alienate moderate and independent voters: there’s actually room for everyone at that table. Why would the party not just let a Democrat’s popularity with voters speak for itself, regardless of whether that candidate represents where establishment Democrats envision the party’s general direction?

Even when it comes to winners like Sen-elect Abdul El-Sayed — who had to grapple with the onslaught of bigoted Republicans and right-wing media outlets trying desperately to establish imaginary ties between him and Islamic extremism — Democrats seemed nervous about throwing their lot in with him until he became too popular with the base to deny his viability. Yet, El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers by seven points, which he predicted would be the outcome.

And it’s not just establishment Democrats who seem to have a problem staying out of their own way. Earlier, I noted that CNN reported that moderate Democrats did better than progressive democrats in terms of the margins they won by. The article I cited was titled, Midterm returns show bad news for progressive Democrats. But why frame it that way? Mind you, this was an article about all the Democrats, moderate and “far left” alike, who won their races. What’s with this narrative that if progressives didn’t beat their opponents down as badly as moderate Dems did, that’s an indication that the party just isn’t ready to shift that far to the left, especially considering the difference in the way many of these candidates were funded?

This isn’t to say that if Nixon won, Florida would have been added to the list of states that miraculously turned blue, but Democrats would have had meant Democrats would have been looking at 55 Senate seats to Republicans’ 43, instead of its 54-44 lead, and that’s still something.

Again, it was a blowout either way you slice it, so this might seem like a petty gripe that isn’t worth griping, but there are other elections to consider in the future, and considering the blue tsunami was shocking for everyone, regardless of what the polls were saying leading up to it, perhaps one lesson to take from it all is this:

If the established Democratic Party just stops kneecapping itself out of some out-of-touch fear that going too far left will lead to its downfall, there’s no telling what the political landscape looks like in 2028 and beyond.

The midterms proved, if nothing else, that the nation is no longer nearly as conservative as we once thought. Why fight that?

news.summary: Democrats may have picked up more congressional seats than they did, if not for their out-of-touch fear of the “far left.”
news.author: Zack Linly

news.title: Biden Downplays Infamous 2024 CNN Debate as ‘Not Very Consequential’
news.text:
The June 27, 2024, debate on CNN intensified concerns about Biden’s age and fitness for office after he struggled to finish sentences and complete some answers. His performance triggered weeks of public scrutiny and pressure from Democratic lawmakers and donors, culminating in his decision to withdraw from the presidential race on July 21. 

The CNN-hosted debate drew 51.3 million viewers across television networks, according to Nielsen, including 9.53 million on CNN itself. The broadcast was CNN’s most-watched program in its history at the time, underscoring the scale of the televised moment that ultimately reshaped the presidential race. Biden’s halting performance, however, quickly became the dominant story of the night, overshadowing much of the candidates’ discussion of policy.

“I had very good relationships with all the major leaders in the world,” Biden said. “And so I believe that on an objective basis I was the best-equipped person to do the job.”

Jill Biden also defended the decision to seek another term, explaining that her husband had initially considered leaving office after one term. But Democrats’ stronger-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms encouraged him to continue, she said.

“Everybody kept saying, ‘No, you’ve won the midterms. You’re doing so great. Look at all we’re doing. We have work to continue,’” she recalled.

Biden’s withdrawal came just 24 days after the debate, following repeated efforts to reassure voters and Democratic leaders that he could serve another four years. He subsequently endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris, who became the Democratic nominee and lost to Trump in November 2024.

The former president says he expected another debate with Donald Trump, despite the fallout that ultimately derailed his reelection campaign

The legitimacy of whether Trump himself wrote the note has come into question.

news.title: After Democratic sweep, Texas looms as “big kahuna”  in the 2028 presidential race
news.text:
WASHINGTON — The day after Democrats swept every statewide office in Texas, Sen. Ted Cruz went on his podcast and laid down a promise. 

“I give you my word: Texas will be red again,” he said.

The chair of the Democratic National Committee had a different read. Asked whether he considers Texas a battleground state in the next presidential contest, Ken Martin said in an interview, “For sure — it’s seismic.”

Just two years after President Donald Trump carried Texas by nearly 14 percentage points, Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted Gov. Greg Abbott while James Talarico won the state’s U.S. Senate race by 12 points, showing how quickly the ground can shift here. The 2028 presidential election will be the first and most consequential test of whether that was an outlier or the beginning of a more permanent change. 

At stake is a remaking of the presidential map. With 40 electoral votes, Texas is the second-biggest prize in the Electoral College and the anchor for every Republican presidential candidate since 1980. Without Texas, the path to 270 Electoral College votes is near impossible for Republicans — and after the 2030 Census, the state is poised to gain even more electors.

For decades, neither party’s presidential nominees have had to fight for it. Democrats, who last won a presidential race in Texas with Jimmy Carter, have treated the state as little more than a fundraising pit stop. In their absence, Republican candidates have won the state relatively easily and rarely showed up either.

Now the results of last week’s wave are a political Rorschach test, where prospective candidates and party figures alike see an opportunity.

Karl Rove, the architect of decades’ worth of Republican victories in Texas and George W. Bush’s chief political strategist, said Texas’ competitiveness in 2028 will turn on a few key factors that will come into focus in the coming years.

“The question is going to be, does the Republican Party get its act together by 2028?” Rove said. “And the other question is going to be, is the Democratic Party going to govern from the center, or are they going to be a bunch of Austin liberals? And then the third question is going to be, who do the respective parties nominate in 2028?”

The Democratic victory was neither a fluke nor a “dramatic overnight change in the composition of the Texas electorate,” Rove said, noting that Democratic victories were powered in part by significant crossover voting from Republicans and red-leaning independents registering their opposition to a ticket led by embattled GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton.

Cruz, a potential presidential candidate himself, sees the results as a wake-up call for the GOP to recenter on the economy.

“We will bring Texas back,” Cruz said on his podcast the day after the election, enunciating each word. “I am filled with hope and optimism. Texas will be red again. We have not suddenly become a bunch of tofu-eating, gun-banning, tutu-wearing, pinko commie liberals. That ain’t us. Texas is still Texas. We will rebuild as a true blue-collar party — not by embracing socialism, but by being real free market conservatives.”

Martin, the DNC chair, said Democrats’ midterm sweep in Texas creates “opportunities to actually expand out the map into parts of the country that have not typically been key parts of our strategy, and now will be.” And Rove acknowledged last Tuesday’s results may bring more Democratic investment and interest into the state — and that Republicans should be ready for it.

But the amount of donor money and party attention doesn’t always translate into victories. Democrats, Rove said, had plenty of money and a significant apparatus in Texas for decades, but that didn’t stop Republican momentum.

“I was the young kid in 1980 when we were a battleground state,” Rove said of the year he served as Ronald Reagan’s Texas state director. “The Democrat apparatus was bigger and stronger than the Republican apparatus. And we won.”

How Democrats govern

For Democrats, having one of their own in the Texas governor’s mansion could unlock resources and a platform for the blue team in 2028, particularly if Democrats are able to deliver on their campaign promises using their new governing majorities both on the state and federal levels.

Hinojosa “ran for this job for one reason only, which was to help Texans,” Martin said. “But let me say selfishly, as chair of the national party, she’s going to play a huge role, because she is now governor of one of the largest states, one of the most important states. She will have a huge role in what happens in ’28.”

Texas Democrats across the board, especially Hinojosa, ran on populist platforms focused on lowering costs, boosting public education, curbing Big Tech development and eliminating government corruption. But while Democrats took control of the Texas House and governor’s mansion for the first time in decades, Republicans still hold a majority in the state Senate and are likely to throw up roadblocks limiting the sweep of Democrats’ agenda.

“Come 2027, a whole new generation of Democratic office holders will have the opportunity to show their stuff, show Texans what Democratic governance can look like in a way that helps their lives,” said Julián Castro, the former San Antonio mayor, U.S. secretary of housing and urban development and 2020 Democratic presidential candidate.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a widely anticipated 2028 contender, said in an interview that he does see Texas as a battleground moving forward, and that he expected “major investment by both parties” in the state. 

“Those of us who want to see a change in the country know that Texas is the avenue through which change can occur that’ll make a big difference for the rest of the country,” he said.

Pritzker visited Texas several times this cycle and donated $1.2 million in support of Hinojosa’s bid, a level of individual support that fueled a kind of national proxy war. Numerous Latino Democrats criticized Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, another anticipated 2028 contender and chair of the Democratic Governors Association, for declining to invest more into her race. Pritzker, a billionaire whose family founded Hyatt hotels, also previously hosted dozens of Texas Democratic lawmakers in Illinois when they walked out of the Legislature to protest Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting scheme in 2025.

“Democrats can’t win the presidency or the Congress unless we’re winning in places that are not just blue states,” Pritzker said, pointing to Georgia’s evolution into a blue state beginning in 2020 as a “signal” that investing in GOP-controlled states in the South could pay off. “Texas is the biggest. It’s the big kahuna.”

And even the perception of competitiveness could compel Republicans to divert resources from more traditional battlegrounds to preserving their win streak in a state they cannot afford to lose.

Republicans in the state have long feared that one Democratic statewide win would trigger a flood of donor money and interest to a state most Democrats had long since written off. The 2026 sweep could open the floodgates.

Who the parties nominate

Talarico himself expressed caution against reading the 2026 results as a shift in the partisanship of the state. But he said Texas is “absolutely” on the map for the next presidential race.

“I think this shows that if candidates run in Texas who connect with Texans, who speak to their needs, who build a big tent, they can absolutely be successful in our state,” Talarico told Politico last week. “And I would urge every 2028 candidate to vigorously compete in our state.”

Such a campaign would mark a stark difference from past cycles, when presidential activity in Texas has tended to dry up after Super Tuesday.

Vice President Kamala Harris made all of one post-Labor Day campaign stop there in 2024, for an event with Houston native Beyoncé. Despite losing by less than 6 percentage points in 2020, Joe Biden never visited Texas that fall. And Hillary Clinton never visited in the 2016 general election.

Across his three runs, Trump hosted three rallies and gave one speech in 2016, and made zero general election campaign visits in 2020 or 2024. Mitt Romney in 2012 visited for a number of fundraisers but only three public events. And John McCain spent two days in Texas during the 2008 general election, delivering one speech.

Castro said it was a combination of limited resources, the presence of Texas Republicans on the ticket and unfavorable data that kept Texas off of the battleground map for decades.

Even after last week, winning the state’s 40 electoral votes remains an enormous lift for any Democrat, given its expensive nature and fundamental partisan lean. But Castro expects 2028 to be different: more candidate visits, more attention and more resources for November, not just Super Tuesday. 

“I don’t think anybody expects 2028 in Texas to be as favorable as 2026 was, since 2026 was a once-in-a-lifetime wipeout for Republicans. But, I’m convinced that it’s going to be much more competitive than it has been in the past,” Castro said.

Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn contended that Republicans lost his home state largely because their brand was tarnished among key voter blocs. Texas, he said, is “still center-right and basically red except for these extraordinary circumstances.”

“I think people lost confidence in the Republicans because of their tolerance for corruption, both at the state level and at the national level,” Cornyn said. “But Democrats need to be careful, because I don’t think — Texas didn’t turn blue. This wasn’t a mandate for them, this was a referendum on the status quo. So, it’ll be fascinating to watch.”

Candidate quality, Rove noted, cuts both ways and will matter greatly for 2028.

If Republicans nominate someone who can adhere to and strengthen the party’s old school appeal — economic growth, good schools, limited government, strong national defense and traditional values among them — then Rove is confident the state will return to its Republican nature. In a Democratic field expected to be sizable, the nominee will determine if Texas is in play.

“They nominate the governor of California? That’s not going to be helpful in Texas,” Rove said. “The question is, can they nominate somebody who’s going to be a moderate, a moderate centrist Democrat, traditional Democrat. Then they might have a shot.”

Texas’ newfound blue streak will also matter for Cruz, who has teased a presidential bid in recent months and taken an occasional swipe at presumed frontrunner JD Vance. As one of the few statewide Republicans still in office, he is well-positioned to lead the party back to power. 

To that end, Cruz allies launched a nonprofit called Saving Texas, headquartered in Austin, a week after the election, to focus on rebuilding the GOP’s candidate bench, infrastructure and war chest. On his podcast after the election, Cruz committed to “pouring every breath, every strength in my body” into Republicans’ comeback effort in Texas.

Texans have been on a major-party presidential ticket in eight elections since 1960. In each case, the party whose ticket included a Texan won the state — though in 1988, both tickets had one, with George H.W. Bush beating Michael Dukakis and his running mate, Texas Sen. Lloyd Bentsen.

On the other hand, Hinojosa’s win means that, if Cruz were to win the 2028 election, she would get to appoint his temporary replacement until a special election could be held. However, Cruz’s Senate seat is not up until 2030, so a loss in the Republican primaries or general election would not impact Republican control of the seat.

And Cruz is not the only Texan who could warrant presidential attention. If Texas is truly competitive, its electoral weight could convince the eventual Democratic nominee to want a Texan on the ticket, Castro said.

“I expect that both Talarico and Hinojosa will be very seriously considered as vice presidential nominees, under the theory that they can help carry Texas,” Castro said.
news.summary: Presidential nominees have long skipped Texas. But Democrats, fresh off defeating Gov. Greg Abbott and winning the U.S. Senate race, are taking a second look.
news.author: Gabby Birenbaum

news.title: Scarlett Johansson is on the hunt for something deeper
news.text: It's election day morning and, with voters poised to reshape the country's political landscape, Scarlett Johansson is still trying to figure out when she'll have time to vote. Speaking by phone from her home in New York City, the 41-year-old actor laughs as she resigns herself to probably voting at "prime time," when she expects the lines to be longest. Johansson, who helped assemble her fellow "Avengers" stars for a video supporting Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, is feeling anxious but hopeful. "I feel like we're living in such a weird dystopian time — there are so many things stressing me out in the zeitgeist," she says. "Hopefully there will be a historic turnout and things will positively change." As it turned out, Democrats won both houses of Congress in a historic midterm landslide. Johansson has plenty on her plate. Fresh off Halloween with her daughter Rose, 12, and son Cosmo, 5, she's about to start shooting "Scapegoat," the new film from "Hereditary" director Ari Aster (more on that later). She's been working virtually nonstop since February, playing a New York homicide detective in Mike Flanagan's upcoming "The Exorcist: Martyrs" and taking on a still-secret role opposite Robert Pattinson in Matt Reeves' "The Batman: Part II." She and her husband, Colin Jost, who is busy with another season of "Saturday Night Live," coordinate their schedules to keep their children's lives as normal as possible. Johansson would love to return to Broadway, where she won a Tony in 2010 for "A View From the Bridge," but says theater is difficult to reconcile with raising young children. "I consider myself the CEO of our household," she says, her famously husky voice instantly recognizable even over the phone. "I'm a hands-on parent. I love being a mom. Kids have so much going on and their lives are important." Johansson's latest film puts that maternal devotion to a far more harrowing test. In "Paper Tiger," a new crime thriller from director James Gray set in 1986, she plays Hester, a Queens mother whose husband, Irwin (Miles Teller), and his former-cop brother Gary (Adam Driver) become involved in a dubious consulting job connected to the Russian mob and Brooklyn's polluted Gowanus Canal. When the deal turns violent, Hester and her two sons find themselves in the mob's crosshairs. At the same time, she is confronting a frightening medical diagnosis that she keeps secret from her family. The Neon film opens in limited release on Friday. Gray, known for emotionally intense, character-driven films like "We Own the Night" (2007) and "The Lost City of Z" (2017), drew on his own family history for "Paper Tiger." He initially envisioned a different version of the story with Anne Hathaway, who had played a character based on his mother in 2022's "Armageddon Time." But Hathaway was tied up with Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," so Gray reworked the story into something more operatic and turned to Johansson, whose work he had long admired. With her tight perm, oversized glasses and thick outer-borough accent, Johansson’s Hester has a watchful unease as the dangers surrounding her family mount. It's an unusually unglamorous, tightly wound performance, one that allows Johansson to disappear into an ordinary woman's increasingly desperate circumstances. For Gray, much of her portrayal comes down to what she can convey without saying a word. "She has a marvelous face," the director says. "I don't just mean physical attraction. I mean that the camera captures a level of introspection where she doesn't have to say anything, really. I would just film one shot of her listening and it would tell something of the story. That's rare. It's telling you that the actor is always thinking." Johansson sees Hester as a woman who had put aside her youthful ambitions — "as I think many women do," she adds — to devote herself to her family. With her eldest son preparing for college, Hester believes those sacrifices are finally paying off, giving him opportunities she and her husband never had. "That's the American dream, right?" Johansson says. For Gray, the film's most painful element comes directly from his own life. His mother was diagnosed with glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, when he was 18. She tried to shield her husband and sons from the full extent of her illness, but Gray believes the secrecy ultimately damaged their relationships. Watching Johansson re-create aspects of that experience was sometimes almost unbearable for him. "It's like watching a simulacrum of your life," Gray says. "I still dream about my mother from time to time. I don't think you ever get over that kind of loss. She was conjuring it in a very authentic way." Johansson says she didn't realize until preproduction how deeply the story drew on Gray's own family history. Rather than trying to re-create his mother, she imagined Hester becoming increasingly disoriented and terrified as the tumor begins affecting her vision and her husband proves incapable of protecting the family from the danger he's brought into their lives. "It's almost like she's living in an alternate reality," Johansson says. "It's like a nightmare that she can't wake up from." Beyond the film's immediate drama, Gray says Johansson was deeply curious about the generations of Jewish immigrant history that shaped Hester's family and their aspirations for a better life. It's territory that Johansson has explored in other recent projects. In 2019's "Jojo Rabbit," she played a German mother secretly sheltering a Jewish girl from the Nazis, earning an Oscar nomination for supporting actress (she was also nominated for lead actress that same season for Noah Baumbach's "Marriage Story"). Last year, she made her directorial debut with "Eleanor the Great," about an elderly woman who begins passing off her late friend's Holocaust survival story as her own. Johansson, whose mother is Jewish and father is Danish, sees these stories as part of a broader interest in identity. Raising two children while watching her own parents grow older, she's become increasingly curious about intergenerational trauma and how experiences are passed down through families. "You're in that sort of sandwich generation," she says. "You have a more fully formed perspective on your parents' experience." That curiosity carries over into her acting. "At this stage in my work, I'm interested in the deeper element of, you know: How did I get here? What makes me this way?" Few actors of her generation have moved as comfortably between the machinery of blockbuster filmmaking and the more unpredictable corners of independent cinema. As Black Widow in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, she became one of Hollywood's biggest box-office draws, but she has also repeatedly challenged audiences' expectations, playing an enigmatic alien seductress in Jonathan Glazer's "Under the Skin," an unseen artificial intelligence in Spike Jonze's "Her" and a succession of eccentric mystery women for Wes Anderson. Through it all, Johansson says her instincts about choosing roles haven't changed much since she was a teenager making "Ghost World." "I'm still trying to make things I think are cool," she says. "Or maybe going to be cool. Sometimes you sign up for something and it's going to be cool — and then it's not as cool as you thought it was going to be. That happens too, right?" For Johansson, the rhythms of an actor's life were established early. "I remember going with my fax pages, taking the train with my mom to Times Square and going on castings after school," she says. "Eating a tuna sandwich in Howard Johnson's afterward and then picking up sheet music next door for vocal lessons. Going to Lee Strasberg on Saturdays. It's all I've ever done." She still can imagine finding satisfaction in other fields — medicine, psychology, design — but the idea of giving up acting is almost impossible to comprehend. "It would be like asking a painter what they would do if they didn't paint," she says. "It's just totally woven into the fabric of my entire life." Directing offered Johansson the chance to learn something new after more than three decades on movie sets. She hopes to do it again, though she's in no rush. "I just want to make sure I find something where the lemon’s worth the squeeze." Johansson has considerable clout — and a history of using it. In 2021, she sued Disney over its decision to release "Black Widow" simultaneously in theaters and on streaming, arguing that the move deprived her of box-office bonuses. The dispute was settled out of court. Three years later, she publicly challenged OpenAI after it unveiled a chatbot voice she said sounded eerily similar to hers, despite her having declined an offer to lend her voice to the company. OpenAI denied copying her voice but withdrew it nonetheless. Having navigated Hollywood since childhood, Johansson knows that sustaining a career requires more than talent, particularly in an industry that can be unforgiving to female actors as they get older. With studios struggling to draw audiences to theaters, she thinks carefully about whether a movie can actually connect with moviegoers. "Am I making something that other people want to see? Is there an audience for this movie?" she says. "I'm not making a movie just for me." She sometimes goes further, questioning whether a studio should make a movie at all. "Sometimes I get studio projects that I have to say, 'I don't think you should make this. I don't know who you're making this for,' " she says. " 'It seems irresponsible to make this.' " Earlier in her career, Johansson says, she sometimes felt she needed a commercial hit to reach the next level. But having achieved just about everything an actor could hope for, what is the next level? Asked how her idea of success has changed over the years, she pauses, struggling briefly to find an answer. "It's a good question," she says. "My aspirations are maybe different now. I've been kind of contemplating that too. I think I'm sort of in the middle of that." Whatever direction she takes, Johansson has no shortage of work ahead, including Aster's "Scapegoat," which co-stars Jacob Elordi and Jude Law. The director of "Midsommar" and "Beau Is Afraid" has kept his plot a closely guarded secret. Depending on which rumors you believe, it's either a thriller about a doctor performing surgery on a social media star or a sci-fi romance. "I don't know what it is either," she says. "I'll have more information for you after a few weeks." But she's clearly excited by what Aster has conceived. "The script is just so intense," she says. "It has this immediacy to it that is really different. I've never read anything like it before." She found herself repeatedly shocked by it. "Colin was like, 'What are you reading?' Because I kept going, 'Oh, my God!' " For all the uncertainty about what comes next, the experience of acting itself remains a powerful draw. Johansson describes the exhilaration of working with another actor when they're "soaring together" and every piece of a scene seems to click into place. "Something is happening, alive in a moment, being captured by a camera and 200 crew members witnessing it and participating in it and making it possible," she says. "And it's for these two minutes of film." There's a genuine excitement in her voice as she tries to put the experience into words. "It's why I'm still doing it," she says.
news.summary: After three decades of stardom, Scarlett Johansson has the clout to choose her own path. But as she stars in James Gray's “Paper Tiger,” she's still working out where she wants that path to lead.
